destinations.name: Edinburgh
destinations.summary: A genuinely stunning, walkable capital with a castle, a volcano, and centuries of stone packed into a small footprint, undercut by a Royal Mile that has become one of the most-complained-about tourist traps in the UK, an August that triples hotel prices, and a new 5 percent visitor levy that just started.
destinations.headline: Edinburgh in 2026: gorgeous Old Town, brutal August pricing, a new 5% tourist tax, and a Royal Mile full of traps
destinations.body:
Edinburgh earns its reputation. The Old Town's medieval closes climb up from Princes Street toward a castle perched on an extinct volcano, and Arthur's Seat gives you a genuine hike with a summit view over the whole city, all within a 20 to 30 minute walk of the train station. It photographs as well as anywhere in Europe and it is compact enough to see the highlights on foot in two or three days. That said, treat any description of Edinburgh as effortlessly charming with suspicion, because a lot of the experience now depends on when you show up and how much you plan ahead.

As of 24 July 2026, Edinburgh became the first UK city to charge a visitor levy, a 5 percent surcharge added to paid overnight accommodation for the first five consecutive nights of a stay, projected to raise up to 50 million pounds a year for the city. It applies to bookings made on or after 1 October 2025, so anyone who paid for a stay before that date is exempt even if the trip itself falls in 2026. Budget for it the same way you would a hotel tax anywhere else, but do not be surprised if it appears as a separate line at checkout rather than folded into the quoted room rate.

Edinburgh Castle itself is worth the visit but no longer worth a walk-up ticket. It now runs on 30-minute timed-entry slots, adult online tickets run in the low-to-mid 20s in pounds (roughly 21 to 24 online, more at the gate), and booking online both saves a few pounds and is the only realistic way to guarantee a slot in July or August. Skipping the booking and just showing up in peak season is a good way to lose half a day.

August is the real trap for anyone budgeting loosely. The Fringe Festival runs 7 to 31 August 2026, and it turns Edinburgh into one of the most expensive small cities in Britain for those three and a half weeks. Hostel dorm beds that normally run 20 to 35 pounds jump to 45 to 80, budget chain hotels that are 55 to 140 pounds off-season climb to 150 to 300, and the well-located rooms are typically gone by January or February. If money matters, visit in the shoulder months instead. January through March and November offer 20 to 40 percent discounts on accommodation compared with summer, and the weather in July and August, while the warmest of the year at around 19C by day, still carries real rain risk and can turn cold and windy with little warning, especially up on Arthur's Seat or Calton Hill.

The Royal Mile is the other honest disappointment. It is genuinely picturesque and worth walking once, but it has been named repeatedly as one of the worst tourist traps in the UK, with hundreds of reviews flagging tacky souvenir shops and whisky stores that quote prices on the spot rather than posting them, sometimes well above what the same bottle costs elsewhere. There has also been a documented rise in shoplifting and theft targeting shops along the street, which locals have described as making parts of it feel poorly policed. None of that makes the street dangerous for visitors, but it does mean the tartan shops and whisky tastings closest to the castle are the least trustworthy version of what Scotland actually sells.

Any international visitor who is not a British or Irish citizen and does not already hold UK immigration status now needs a UK Electronic Travel Authorisation before arrival, a requirement that started 25 February 2026. It costs 20 pounds per person as of April 2026, up from 16 pounds, with no discount for children, and it is valid for up to two years. It is a five-minute online application but it is easy to forget since it is separate from a passport and from any US-style ESTA people may already be used to.
destinations.what_great: The Old Town skyline, the castle on its volcanic crag, and Arthur's Seat give Edinburgh a compact, walkable core where genuinely dramatic scenery sits a short walk from the train station, something few European capitals manage. Crime against tourists is low and violent crime is rare, with Police Scotland logging only 47 tourist-related thefts across all of 2025, and the city's museums, closes, and viewpoints reward slow wandering without needing a car or a big budget for entry fees.
destinations.what_ruined: The Royal Mile has curdled into one of the most complained-about tourist traps in the country, with unposted whisky prices and a documented rise in shop theft, and the city's calendar now punishes anyone who cannot travel in the shoulder season, since the Fringe from 7 to 31 August roughly doubles or triples accommodation costs and a new 5 percent visitor levy on top of already-rising hotel and bus fares adds friction that simply did not exist a couple of years ago.
tips: Book Edinburgh Castle online in advance: adult tickets run roughly 21 to 24 pounds online versus more at the gate, and entry is now assigned in 30-minute timed slots that sell out in July and August.

A new 5 percent visitor levy started 24 July 2026 on paid overnight stays for the first five nights; it applies only to bookings made on or after 1 October 2025, so factor it into any hotel quote from now on.

If you are not a British or Irish citizen and lack UK immigration status, apply for a UK ETA before you fly; it costs 20 pounds per person as of April 2026 and takes only minutes online, but it is separate from your passport and easy to forget.

Avoid the Royal Mile's whisky and tartan shops closest to the castle for actual purchases; prices are often quoted verbally rather than posted, and the street has documented theft and overcharging complaints. Buy whisky at a supermarket or a reputable specialist like Royal Mile Whiskies instead.

If the Fringe (7 to 31 August 2026) is not the specific draw, avoid it: budget hotel rates jump from roughly 55 to 140 pounds a night up to 150 to 300, and the best-located rooms are typically booked out by January or February.

Lothian Buses run a flat adult single fare of 2.20 pounds after the February 2026 fare revision, with a day ticket around 4.30 to 4.50 pounds, cheaper than the Airlink airport bus or tram for getting around once you are in the city.

From Edinburgh Airport, the tram runs 7.90 pounds one-way (9.50 pounds open return) and takes about 30 minutes to the city centre; the Airlink 100 bus is 6.00 pounds single (8.50 return), runs 24 hours including when the tram does not, but ask locally about journey time before assuming it is faster.

Visit in June through August for the warmest, driest weather (roughly 19C by day, around 70 to 83 mm of rain a month), or January through March for hotel rates 20 to 40 percent below summer if you can tolerate cold and rain.

guide.title: Edinburgh travel guide 2026: getting in, getting around, and dodging the Fringe-month price spike
guide.summary: A practical rundown of airport transfers, city transit, where to base yourself, and how to plan around the Fringe and the new visitor levy.
guide.body:
Edinburgh Airport sits about 8 miles west of the city centre and has three practical ways in. The tram is the simplest option for anyone staying near Princes Street or the Old Town: it runs directly from the airport concourse to York Place in about 30 minutes, costs 7.90 pounds for a single or 9.50 pounds for an open return, and departs every 7 minutes or so at peak times. The Airlink 100 bus is the budget and 24-hour option, running to Waverley Bridge for 6.00 pounds single or 8.50 pounds return, useful for late-night or early-morning arrivals when the tram is not running. Taxis cost considerably more but are worth it with heavy luggage or a group of three or four splitting the fare.

Once in the city, Edinburgh rewards walking. The Old Town and New Town sit close enough together that most first-time visitors barely need transit for sightseeing, but for anything further out, Lothian Buses run a flat adult single fare of 2.20 pounds citywide following the February 2026 fare revision, with an all-day ticket around 4.30 to 4.50 pounds that pays for itself after two rides. Cobblestones on the Royal Mile and steep closes off it are genuinely punishing in anything other than solid, flat shoes, worth knowing before you pack.

For where to stay, Old Town puts you inside the postcard view but means noise, tourist pricing, and the most theft-prone stretch of the Royal Mile on your doorstep. New Town, just across the valley from the castle, offers Georgian architecture, calmer streets, and easy tram or bus access at broadly similar prices. Leith, the old port district a short bus or tram ride north, has become the value and food-scene alternative, generally 15 to 30 percent cheaper for comparable rooms with a 10 to 15 minute commute into the centre.

If your trip falls anywhere near 7 to 31 August 2026, plan around the Fringe deliberately rather than by accident. It is genuinely one of the world's great arts festivals and worth experiencing once, but budget hotel rates that normally run 55 to 140 pounds a night jump to 150 to 300, mid-range hotels roughly double, and the best-located rooms are typically gone by January or February of that year. Either book seriously early, accept a base outside the centre with a transit commute, or deliberately avoid the dates if a lower-key, cheaper Edinburgh is the goal, shoulder months like May, June, September, or the discounted window of January through March are all reasonable substitutes.

For day trips, Glasgow is the easy one: ScotRail runs direct trains every 15 to 20 minutes between Edinburgh Waverley and Glasgow Queen Street, taking roughly 50 minutes with fares as low as 8.40 pounds one-way if booked ahead. Highlands day tours by coach run considerably longer, 12 hours or more round trip, and are worth it only if a full Highlands trip is not otherwise on the itinerary. On money matters generally, contactless and Apple/Google Pay are accepted almost everywhere including on Lothian Buses, so carrying cash is mostly unnecessary except for the odd small independent shop.

rating_rationale.overall: The core sights, castle, Old Town, Arthur's Seat, are legitimately excellent and easy to reach on foot, but a tourist-trap-heavy Royal Mile and a festival month that reshapes pricing and crowding for a third of the summer keep it from a top score.
rating_rationale.safety: Police Scotland's own 2025 numbers show only 47 tourist-related thefts citywide for the year and violent crime against visitors is rare; pickpocketing in crowded spots like the Royal Mile and Waverley Station is the main real risk, not personal safety.
rating_rationale.value: Outside August, mid-range hotels run roughly 120 to 175 pounds a night and city buses are a flat 2.20 pounds a ride, reasonable for a UK capital, but Fringe-month pricing that can triple room rates plus the new 5 percent visitor levy and rising transit fares pull the average down.

destinations.name: Havana
destinations.summary: Havana's colonial architecture and classic cars are real, but rolling blackouts, a cash-only economy shut off from US cards, and a maze of OFAC rules make it demanding for American travelers.
destinations.headline: Havana in 2026: Gorgeous Colonial Ruins, 12-Hour Blackouts, and a Cash-Only Maze for US Travelers
destinations.body:
Havana is not a normal Caribbean trip for Americans, and the paperwork starts before you book a flight. Pure tourism is not a legal reason to go. US travelers must qualify under one of 12 OFAC-authorized categories, and the most common one, Support for the Cuban People, requires that your spending go to private Cuban businesses like casas particulares and paladares rather than state-run hotels or restaurants. US law also requires travelers to keep receipts, booking confirmations, and an itinerary documenting the trip for five years. In January 2026 the Trump administration issued an executive order reinstating Cuba's State Sponsor of Terrorism designation and tightened travel and remittance rules further, with a second executive order on May 1, 2026 adding sanctions tied to repression in Cuba. None of this makes travel illegal, but it makes the compliance bar higher than it has been in years.

Once you land, the money situation is its own project. Because of the US embargo, credit and debit cards issued by American banks, Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover, do not work anywhere in Cuba. Assume you are paying cash for the entire trip in US dollars, euros, or Cuban pesos. The official exchange rate hovers around 110 Cuban pesos to the dollar, though informal street rates can be more favorable. Entry itself costs money too: US citizens need the pink tourist card, which runs $50 to $100 depending on where it's purchased, while non-US travelers use a green tourist card priced around $25 to $30. Airlines will deny boarding without one.

The most disruptive fact of a 2026 Havana trip is the electrical grid. Cuba has been in the worst power crisis in its history since late 2024, with fuel shortages, a crippled Antonio Guiteras plant, and the loss of subsidized Venezuelan oil driving repeated total grid collapses. On Easter Sunday, April 5, 2026, the national system was generating roughly 1,278 megawatts against peak demand near 3,000 megawatts, a shortfall of more than 1,700 megawatts. In Havana that translates to scheduled and unscheduled outages that can run 12 hours or more a day, hitting air conditioning, water pumps, refrigeration, and wifi alike. Outside the capital it's often worse and longer.

The upside is that the things Havana is famous for still deliver. The 1950s American convertibles cruising the Malecon are real working taxis, and drivers who park along the seafront or Parque Central will quote $25 to $35 an hour if you book directly and negotiate before getting in, versus $60 to $100 an hour through Viator, GetYourGuide, or a hotel concierge for the same ride. The US State Department rates Cuba a Level 2 travel advisory, Exercise Increased Caution, the same tier as France, Germany, and Spain. Petty crime, pickpocketing and bag snatching, is the real risk, concentrated around Old Havana, Obispo Street, and the Malecon after dark, while violent crime against tourists remains rare even as it has ticked up nationally.
destinations.what_great:
The classic-car culture is not a tourist trap dressed up for cameras, it's the actual transportation system, and booking directly with a driver on the Malecon or at Parque Central gets you the same convertible ride for $25 to $35 an hour that platforms charge $60 to $100 for. Old Havana's colonial architecture, the paladares serving genuinely good food for $15 to $25 a person, and casas particulares renting private rooms for $25 to $50 a night with breakfast and hot water included make the on-the-ground experience feel affordable once you've cleared the entry hurdles.

Safety-wise, Havana earns the same Level 2 State Department advisory as major Western European capitals, and violent crime against tourists is genuinely rare. If your main worry is getting mugged, Havana is not the outlier people assume.
destinations.what_ruined:
The electricity crisis is not a minor inconvenience, it's the defining fact of the trip. Rolling blackouts have hit 12 or more hours a day in Havana since the 2024-2026 grid collapse, and on April 5, 2026 the country was producing barely 1,278 megawatts against roughly 3,000 megawatts of demand. That means unpredictable AC, water pressure, refrigeration, and wifi, on top of a cash-only economy that locks out every US-issued card and forces you to carry your entire budget in physical dollars, euros, or pesos.

The bureaucracy stacks on top of that. Americans need a qualifying OFAC travel category, five years of retained receipts, and a $50 to $100 pink tourist card just to enter, and January and May 2026 executive orders tightened the rules further under Cuba's reinstated State Sponsor of Terrorism designation. None of it is insurmountable, but it turns a beach-and-mojito trip into a compliance exercise.
tips: Bring all the cash you'll need in US dollars, euros, or pesos; Visa, Mastercard, Amex, and Discover cards issued by US banks do not work anywhere in Cuba because of the embargo.
Qualify your trip under one of the 12 OFAC travel categories before booking, most tourists use Support for the Cuban People, and keep every receipt and itinerary for five years as US law requires.

Pack a battery bank and a headlamp: Havana blackouts have run 12 or more hours a day since the 2024-2026 grid crisis, and the national grid was producing under half of peak demand as of early April 2026.

Skip the $60-100-an-hour classic car tours sold through Viator or hotel concierges; drivers along the Malecon and Parque Central quote $25-35 an hour for the same convertible ride if you book directly and agree on price first.
US citizens need the pink tourist card ($50-100) rather than the green card non-US travelers use ($25-30); buy it before flying, since airlines deny boarding without it.
Buy Nauta wifi cards at an ETECSA office, like the one on Obispo Street in Old Havana, close to the official $1-2 per hour rate; hotel front desks commonly mark the same cards up three to four times.

guide.title: Havana Travel Guide 2026: Money, Blackouts, and Getting Around
guide.summary: A practical guide to navigating Havana's cash-only economy, chronic power outages, and Cuba entry rules for American travelers.
guide.body:
Getting around Havana mostly means walking Habana Vieja's compact colonial core, then switching to a classic-car taxi or a coco taxi for longer hops to Vedado or Centro Habana. Negotiate the fare before you get in, direct bookings with drivers parked on the Malecon or at Parque Central run $25 to $35 an hour, while the same ride booked through a platform or hotel desk can run $60 to $100. Centro Habana has the highest concentration of budget casas particulares, often $25 to $35 a night for a private room with en suite bathroom in a Cuban family's apartment, while a mid-range room in Old Havana with reliable AC and a private bath runs $35 to $50 booked directly.

Money is the single biggest planning variable. Because US-issued cards do not work anywhere in the country, budget your entire trip in cash, dollars, euros, and Cuban pesos are all usable, and change money at casas or private exchanges rather than relying on the official bank rate, which sits around 110 pesos to the dollar. Factor in the tourist card cost too, $50 to $100 for the pink card US citizens need versus $25 to $30 for the green card other nationalities use, and buy it before your flight since airlines will deny boarding without it.

The power situation should shape your itinerary more than the calendar does. With rolling blackouts hitting 12 or more hours a day in Havana during the ongoing 2024-2026 grid crisis, book accommodations that mention backup generators or battery inverters, keep devices charged whenever the grid is up, and treat consistent wifi and hot water as a bonus rather than a given. For food, paladares, Cuba's private restaurants, consistently outperform state-run restaurants on both quality and price, with a full meal running $15 to $25 a person. For connectivity, buy Nauta wifi cards at an ETECSA office rather than a hotel desk to avoid the standard three-to-four-times markup, and expect 4G coverage to be workable in central neighborhoods but unreliable elsewhere.

rating_rationale.overall: The culture and architecture deliver, but chronic blackouts and heavy US travel bureaucracy pull down what would otherwise be a higher score.
rating_rationale.safety: State Department Level 2, same tier as France and Germany; petty crime in tourist zones is the real risk, violent crime against tourists is rare.
rating_rationale.value: Casas, paladares, and direct-booked car tours are genuinely cheap, but cash-only logistics, card lockout, and mandatory tourist-card fees add real friction and cost.

destinations.name: Hoi An
destinations.summary: UNESCO-listed Vietnamese trading port on the Thu Bon river, known for tailors, lantern nights and heavy autumn flooding. Small, walkable, heavily touristed.
destinations.headline: Hoi An Review: A Genuinely Beautiful Old Town With a Tailor-Shop Hustle and a Flood Season
destinations.body:
Hoi An sits on the Thu Bon river in Quang Nam province, roughly 30 kilometres south of Da Nang, and it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on December 4, 1999 as an exceptionally well preserved Southeast Asian trading port of the 15th to 19th centuries. That listing is earned. The Ancient Town core, essentially Tran Phu, Nguyen Thai Hoc and Bach Dang streets, is a dense grid of ochre shophouses, Chinese assembly halls and the Japanese Covered Bridge, known locally as Chua Cau, which reopened in early August 2024 after a two year restoration costing about 20.2 billion Vietnamese dong, funded equally by Quang Nam province and Hoi An city. The rebuilt bridge drew public criticism for looking too new, and visitors expecting a weathered 400 year old structure should reset expectations.

Access to the heritage core runs on a ticket. Foreign visitors pay 120,000 VND, sold at the small yellow booths at the main entrances, valid 24 hours, and the ticket covers entry to five of the 22 listed heritage buildings, with a tear off strip surrendered at each door. Street level enforcement is inconsistent and many people wander the lanes without buying, but every assembly hall, old house and museum checks it at the door.

Arrival is simple. Da Nang International Airport is the gateway, about 45 minutes out. Grab runs roughly 250,000 to 350,000 VND, plus a small airport pickup surcharge paid directly to the driver, metered taxis land around 300,000 to 400,000 VND, and prearranged private cars sit at 350,000 to 500,000 VND. Touts working the arrivals hall quote 500,000 to 700,000 VND for the identical trip, so use the app or the official rank and decline everything else.

Timing decides the quality of the visit. February to April is the dependable window, warm and dry with low humidity. May to August stays dry but gets genuinely punishing, with highs approaching 40C. September to November is typhoon and flood season on the central coast, and this is not an abstraction. On October 30, 2025 the Thu Bon crested at 5.62 metres in Hoi An, 14 centimetres above the 1964 record, and water only drained out of the Ancient Town on October 31, leaving thick mud through the shophouses. Bach Dang, Nguyen Thai Hoc and Tran Phu, the exact streets visitors come for, sit lowest and flood first. November 2025 brought a second round of inundation.

The lantern night, Dem Ram Pho Co, falls on the 14th night of each lunar month. Remaining 2026 dates include 27 July, 26 August, 24 September, 23 October, 22 November and 22 December. Motorbikes are cleared from the core around 5:30 pm, electric lighting goes down between roughly 6 and 10 pm, and the candle boat release on the Hoai river peaks between 7 and 9 pm.

Outside town, My Son Sanctuary, the Cham temple complex about 50 kilometres inland, charges 150,000 VND for foreigners, which covers the site museum, the electric shuttle to the temple groups and the traditional dance performance.

The honest caveat is commerce. Tailoring is Hoi An's signature industry and also its best documented problem. Hotel staff, drivers and friendly strangers routinely collect 20 to 40 percent commission for delivering a customer to a particular shop, and that cut comes out of either the price or the garment. Suits quoted under 100 US dollars are typically fused rather than canvassed, and synthetic blends are regularly sold to visitors as mulberry silk. A suit promised in 24 hours is usually a modified off the rack piece from a volume factory. None of this makes Hoi An a bad destination. It makes it a place where the visitor who books a tailor directly, allows three or four days for real fittings, and treats the first quoted number as an opening position ends up with a completely different trip from the one who does not.
destinations.what_great: The heritage core is the real thing, a dense grid of 15th to 19th century shophouses and Chinese assembly halls on Tran Phu and Nguyen Thai Hoc that earned UNESCO listing in December 1999. The scale is walkable and bicycle friendly, with An Bang beach a flat 10 to 20 minute ride away. Lantern nights on the 14th of each lunar month shut the core to traffic and kill the electric lighting between roughly 6 and 10 pm. My Son Sanctuary is a legitimate half day at 150,000 VND.
destinations.what_ruined: Tailoring runs on commission, with hotel staff, drivers and strangers taking 20 to 40 percent for steering you to a shop, money that comes straight out of fabric quality. Suits under 100 dollars are fused, polyester is sold as mulberry silk, and 24 hour turnaround means factory garments. Airport touts quote 500,000 to 700,000 VND for a 300,000 VND ride. September to November is flood season: the Thu Bon hit a record 5.62 metres on October 30, 2025, and flooded again in November. Foreigner pricing is routine.
tips: Buy the Ancient Town ticket at the yellow booths for 120,000 VND; it is valid 24 hours and covers five of the 22 listed heritage buildings via tear-off coupons.
Book a tailor yourself rather than through your hotel or driver, because the referral commission of 20 to 40 percent comes out of your fabric quality or your price.
Aim for February to April, when central Vietnam is warm and dry, and avoid September to November, when the Thu Bon flooded to a record 5.62 metres on October 30, 2025.
From Da Nang airport use Grab at roughly 250,000 to 350,000 VND plus a small airport pickup surcharge, and refuse touts quoting 500,000 to 700,000 VND.
Time your visit to a lantern night on the 14th of the lunar month, with 2026 dates including 24 September and 23 October, when motorbikes clear around 5:30 pm and lights go off from about 6 to 10 pm.
Budget a full 150,000 VND for the My Son Sanctuary ticket, which already covers the site museum, the electric shuttle and the Cham dance performance, and go at opening to beat the heat.

guide.title: Hoi An Practical Guide: Tickets, Da Nang Transfers, Flood Months and Tailor Rules
guide.summary: Month by month timing, real Da Nang airport transfer costs, current Ancient Town and My Son ticket prices, daily budget bands, and how the tailor commission system actually works.
guide.body:
When to go is the single decision that matters most in Hoi An. February through April is the strongest window, with warm days, low humidity and very little rain. May through August is reliably dry but hot, with central Vietnam highs pushing toward 40C, which makes midday walking through the Ancient Town unpleasant and pushes most activity to early morning and after dark. September through November is typhoon and flood season on the central coast and is the period to avoid if the trip is inflexible. The 2025 season was the clearest possible illustration: the Thu Bon river reached 5.62 metres in Hoi An on October 30, 2025, 14 centimetres higher than the 1964 record, floodwater sat in the Ancient Town until October 31, and a second round of flooding hit in early November. December and January are cooler and drier than October and November but still fall inside the wet season, so beach days are unreliable.

Getting in means Da Nang International Airport, roughly 30 kilometres and about 45 minutes north. Grab is the cleanest option at roughly 250,000 to 350,000 VND, with a small airport pickup surcharge handed to the driver on top of the in app fare. A metered taxi from the official rank, Mai Linh among them, generally runs 300,000 to 400,000 VND. A prearranged private transfer or hotel car costs 350,000 to 500,000 VND and is worth it on a late arrival. Freelance touts inside and outside arrivals quote 500,000 to 700,000 VND for the same ride. Decline them, walk to the rank, or open the app.

Getting around town is deliberately easy. The Ancient Town is small and closed to motorbikes during the pedestrian hours, so bicycles, usually free from hotels, cover almost everything including the 10 to 20 minute flat ride east to An Bang and Cua Dai beaches. Grab bikes and cars work for longer runs.

For sites, start with the Ancient Town ticket itself: 120,000 VND for foreigners, sold at yellow booths at the main entrances, valid 24 hours, admitting you to five of the 22 listed heritage buildings via tear off coupons. Spend the coupons on the assembly halls and old merchant houses rather than the smallest museums. The Japanese Covered Bridge, Chua Cau, reopened in August 2024 after a restoration costing about 20.2 billion VND, and it is worth seeing while accepting that the finish is visibly new and has been publicly criticised for exactly that. My Son Sanctuary, about 50 kilometres inland, charges 150,000 VND for foreigners, which includes the site museum, the electric shuttle and the dance show, and is best done on an early morning departure before the heat and the tour buses converge. Try to line the trip up with a lantern night, Dem Ram Pho Co, on the 14th night of the lunar month, with 2026 dates including 27 July, 26 August, 24 September, 23 October, 22 November and 22 December: motorbikes clear around 5:30 pm, electric lights go off from roughly 6 to 10 pm, and candle boats peak on the water between 7 and 9 pm. The one thing worth skipping is any tailor visit arranged by a driver or hotel desk.

On budget, the fixed and verifiable costs are modest. The Ancient Town ticket is 120,000 VND, My Son is 150,000 VND, and the airport transfer is 250,000 to 500,000 VND each way. At roughly 25,000 VND to the US dollar, that is about 5 dollars, 6 dollars and 10 to 20 dollars respectively. Around those numbers, a realistic all in daily figure is about 35 to 55 dollars for a budget traveller in a guesthouse eating at street stalls and local markets, about 70 to 120 dollars for a mid range visitor in a boutique hotel with sit down meals and a day trip, and 200 dollars and up if a tailored wardrobe or a riverside resort enters the picture. Treat clothing as a separate line, not a daily one.

Hoi An sees very little violent crime, so the safety conversation here is really about scams and weather, not personal danger. The commission system is the core issue: hotel staff, taxi drivers and helpful strangers earn 20 to 40 percent for steering customers to specific tailors, and that money comes out of fabric quality or your price. Suits under 100 dollars are fused rather than canvassed, polyester is sold as mulberry silk, and 24 hour turnaround means a factory made garment altered to fit. Book tailors independently, insist on multiple fittings across three or four days, and pay a deposit rather than the full amount up front. Agree fares before riding with non metered drivers, expect a foreigner price on unlabelled market goods, and during flood months check river conditions before committing to a riverside hotel.

rating_rationale.overall: The Ancient Town is a genuinely intact 15th to 19th century trading port with UNESCO inscription since December 1999, but the tailoring and souvenir economy is intense enough to shape the whole experience.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime is not the concern here; the real hazards are commercial pressure and a documented flood season, including the October 30, 2025 Thu Bon crest of 5.62 metres that put the Ancient Town underwater.
rating_rationale.value: Core costs are low, with a 120,000 VND Ancient Town ticket, a 150,000 VND My Son entry and a roughly 250,000 to 350,000 VND Grab from Da Nang airport, though commission-driven tailoring can inflate a trip quickly.

destinations.name: Hong Kong
destinations.summary: World-class transit and skyline views at mainland-beating prices, but a March 2026 law now lets police demand your phone password at the border, and it is not a bluff.
destinations.headline: Hong Kong in 2026: the transit is unbeatable, the harbour view is free, and yes, they can make you unlock your phone
destinations.body:
Hong Kong still runs on the best urban transit system most travelers will ever use, and none of it requires guesswork. An adult On-Loan Octopus card costs HK$150 at any MTR Customer Service Centre, including the one inside Hong Kong International Airport, which breaks down as a HK$50 refundable deposit plus HK$100 of starting balance. Visitors who do not want to deal with a deposit refund can instead buy a no-deposit Tourist Octopus for HK$39. Single MTR and bus fares run roughly HK$3 to HK$30 depending on distance, and paying with Octopus is consistently cheaper than buying single-journey paper tickets. The Airport Express into town costs HK$130 to Hong Kong Station at the counter, or HK$120 with an Octopus card, with cheaper stops at Kowloon Station (HK$115, or HK$105 with Octopus) and Tsing Yi (HK$80, or HK$73 with Octopus).

Entry itself has gotten simpler on paper. Hong Kong eliminated arrival and departure card requirements entirely on October 16, 2024, for all travelers, and immigration now processes entries using airline-submitted passenger information instead. Visa-free access covers roughly 170 countries, with US, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand, and most EU passport holders getting up to 90 days, UK citizens getting a notably generous 180 days, and Indian passport holders getting 14 days but only after completing a free online Pre-Arrival Registration, whose minimum applicant age dropped from 11 to 7 as of January 19, 2026.

The real 2026 story, though, is a legal change that has nothing to do with queues or fares. On March 23, 2026, Hong Kong's government revised the implementing rules under the National Security Law to make it a criminal offense to refuse to hand over passwords or decryption assistance for personal electronic devices, phones and laptops included, when demanded by police. The rule applies to everyone present in Hong Kong, including tourists and passengers merely transiting the airport, no judicial warrant is required for the demand, and refusal carries up to six months in jail and a fine of up to HK$100,000. The US State Department, alongside several other governments, issued heightened travel guidance in response, and Hong Kong's existing advisory level sits at Level 2, exercise increased caution, largely because of arbitrary enforcement of local security laws.

On cost, Hong Kong remains flatly more expensive than mainland China across dining, hotels, and most day-to-day spending, though it rewards travelers who eat where locals eat. A cha chaan teng meal runs about HK$58 to HK$120, dim sum for one is HK$120 to HK$250, and fine dining starts around HK$1,500 per person before a mandatory 10 percent service charge kicks in at upscale spots. Hotels range from roughly HK$348 a night in hostels to HK$1,400-plus at the luxury end, with harbourfront rooms in Central commonly landing between HK$1,500 and HK$2,500 a night, and a reintroduced 3 percent hotel accommodation tax applies on top of the room rate. The Peak Tram, still the classic Victoria Peak run, now charges HK$82 one way or HK$116 return for adults after a fare increase that landed harder on children's and seniors' tickets, which rose nearly 40 percent to HK$52 one way and HK$75 return.
destinations.what_great:
The transit system is genuinely the best reason to visit. Octopus works across MTR, buses, ferries and most convenience stores with almost no friction, the Airport Express gets you into Central in about 24 minutes, and Hong Kong scrapped its arrival card entirely in October 2024 so getting through immigration is faster than it used to be. Since December 2025, transit passengers with at least seven hours between flights can even take a free guided airport tour along one of three themed routes with an English-speaking guide, which is a real way to turn a long layover into something useful.

The city also delivers a genuine high-low split that few places manage. You can eat extremely well at a cha chaan teng for the price of a fast food meal back home, then ride the Peak Tram up for a Victoria Harbour skyline view that costs nothing once you are up there, or splurge on Michelin-level dining a few blocks away. Visa-free access for most Western passports up to 90 days, and 180 days for UK citizens, means most travelers can plan a trip with zero visa paperwork.
destinations.what_ruined:
The single biggest problem with visiting Hong Kong right now is not price, it is the March 23, 2026 change to National Security Law enforcement rules. Police can now demand the password or decryption help for any personal device, phone or laptop, from anyone in the territory, including a tourist just transiting the airport, without a warrant, and refusing is a jailable offense. That is a real, current legal risk that did not exist a couple of years ago and it has pushed multiple governments, including the US, to sharpen their travel guidance.

Cost is the other honest friction point. Hong Kong is simply more expensive than mainland China for dining and lodging, hotel rooms near the harbour regularly run HK$1,500 to HK$2,500 a night before the reintroduced 3 percent hotel tax, and the Peak Tram just raised its fares again, hitting children's and seniors' tickets with an almost 40 percent jump. None of it is a scam, it is just a genuinely expensive city that charges accordingly.
tips: Buy the no-deposit Tourist Octopus for HK$39 if you do not want to deal with reclaiming the HK$50 deposit on the standard HK$150 On-Loan Octopus before you fly out.
Tap into the Airport Express with an Octopus card instead of buying a counter ticket, it drops the Hong Kong Station fare from HK$130 to HK$120.

Assume any device you carry can be searched: as of March 23, 2026 refusing to give police your phone or laptop password is a criminal offense with up to six months in jail, so travel with only what you are comfortable unlocking.
If you hold an Indian passport, complete the free Pre-Arrival Registration online before you fly, it is required in addition to the 14-day visa-free allowance and now covers applicants as young as 7.
Skip hotel restaurants for cha chaan teng diners, a full local meal runs about HK$58 to HK$120 versus HK$1,500-plus per person at fine dining spots.
Book Peak Tram tickets in advance if possible since 2026 fare increases pushed adult return tickets to HK$116 and child and senior tickets rose nearly 40 percent to HK$75 return.

guide.title: Hong Kong Practical Guide: Transit, Timing, and What Things Actually Cost in 2026
guide.summary: How to move around Hong Kong cheaply, when the weather and crowds actually cooperate, and where the real money goes.
guide.body:
Getting around is the easiest part of a Hong Kong trip. Buy an Octopus card the moment you land, either the standard HK$150 On-Loan version with its refundable HK$50 deposit or the no-deposit HK$39 Tourist Octopus, and use it on the MTR, buses, ferries, and most convenience stores for the rest of the trip. The Airport Express is the fastest way into town, reaching Hong Kong Station in around 24 minutes for HK$120 with Octopus, and from there the MTR network covers almost everything a visitor needs, with typical single fares landing between HK$3 and HK$30 depending on distance.

Timing matters more than most guides admit. Hong Kong's climate swings hard between a hot, humid, typhoon-prone summer and a cooler, drier autumn and early winter that most travelers find far more comfortable for walking the harbourfront or riding the Peak Tram. Autumn also tends to bring clearer skies for the Victoria Peak skyline views that are the city's signature free attraction once you have paid the tram fare up.

Neighborhood choice changes your budget more than almost anything else. Central and the harbourfront near Victoria Harbour deliver the postcard views but also the HK$1,500 to HK$2,500 nightly hotel rates, plus a 3 percent hotel accommodation tax that was reintroduced in 2025 and still applies. Staying slightly further out, in areas like Mong Kok or Sham Shui Po in Kowloon, cuts lodging costs sharply while keeping you a short, cheap MTR ride from everything, and it puts you closer to the cha chaan teng diners and dim sum spots where a full meal costs a fraction of what a hotel restaurant charges.

On paperwork, the process is genuinely lighter than it used to be. Hong Kong dropped its arrival card requirement entirely in October 2024, so most visitors from visa-free countries walk straight through immigration using only their passport and the airline's advance passenger information. The one real complication is the March 2026 change to device-search powers under the National Security Law, which now lets police demand phone or laptop passwords from anyone in the territory without a warrant, so treat your devices with the same caution you would in any jurisdiction with broad search authority, and keep sensitive data backed up elsewhere rather than carried on the device itself.

rating_rationale.overall: World-class transit, simplified entry, and a real high-low dining and sightseeing split make it a strong destination despite the friction.
rating_rationale.safety: Low street crime but US State Dept keeps Hong Kong at Level 2, and the March 2026 warrantless device-password law is a concrete new legal risk for visitors.
rating_rationale.value: Genuinely more expensive than mainland China on hotels and dining, though Octopus transit and street-level food keep a budget trip possible.

destinations.name: Istanbul
destinations.summary: Istanbul delivers 2,500 years of layered history for a fraction of what a comparable European capital costs, but rapid lira inflation, aggressive taxi scams, and genuine earthquake risk mean the trip requires more homework than the postcards suggest.
destinations.headline: Istanbul in 2026: staggering history, rising prices, and scams you need to plan around before you land
destinations.body:
Istanbul is the only major city straddling two continents, and the density of world-class sights in a walkable radius, Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapi Palace, the Grand Bazaar, is hard to match anywhere. That said, the city has changed fast. Turkey's inflation has run above 30 percent through 2025, and hotel, restaurant, and attraction prices have climbed accordingly, with tourism industry data showing a roughly 5 percent drop in visitor arrivals in July 2025 as travelers balked at costs that now rival or exceed Greece and Spain.

The big sights are no longer casual walk-ins. Hagia Sophia has charged foreign visitors a separate entry fee since January 2024, currently 25 euros for access to the upper gallery museum area, payable in euros or lira, with children under 8 free. Topkapi Palace costs 2,750 Turkish lira at the gate for the combined Palace, Harem, and Hagia Irene ticket, roughly 55 euros, and closes on Tuesdays. The Blue Mosque, by contrast, remains free with no ticket required, but it is an active mosque that shuts to tourists roughly five times a day for prayer and stays closed until around 14:30 on Fridays for the main congregational prayer, so plan around the schedule rather than showing up whenever.

Getting into the city from the airport is where a lot of trips go sideways. Istanbul Airport (IST) taxi ranks have a documented pattern of complaints, meters that run long routes, invented toll charges, and drivers claiming the card machine is broken to force cash payment, with tourist reviews describing this behavior into 2025. Stick to the official taxi queue, insist the meter is running, or use the HAVAIST shuttle bus, about 275 lira one way and card-or-app only since HAVAIST stopped accepting cash. From Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) on the Asian side, the HAVABUS to Taksim runs about 440 lira in cash, with roughly a 100 lira surcharge if you pay by card, and takes about 90 minutes.

Getting around the city itself is cheap relative to Western Europe even after the price hikes. An Istanbulkart transit card costs 130 lira to buy, and a single ride on metro, tram, bus, or ferry starts at 27 lira, dropping to 19.33, then 14.67, then as low as 9.27 lira for additional transfers within the same trip window. Entry requirements depend heavily on nationality: EU, UK, Japanese, and several other passport holders currently enter visa-free for up to 90 days, while US, Canadian, Australian, and many other travelers need an e-Visa, obtainable only at the official evisa.gov.tr site for about 50 dollars, valid 180 days for a 90-day stay. Third-party sites that charge more for the same e-Visa are a real problem, so bookmark the official URL before you go.

Two background realities are worth knowing rather than ignoring. Turkey passed a controversial 2024 law requiring municipalities to remove stray dogs from the streets into shelters, and Istanbul's governor's office pushed a city-wide roundup deadline in 2025, so the free-roaming cats and dogs the city was famous for are visibly fewer and the topic is politically charged locally. Separately, Istanbul sits roughly 20 kilometers from the North Anatolian Fault, one of the world's most active fault lines; a magnitude 6.2 quake hit the Marmara Sea area in April 2025, and geoscientists have estimated as high as a 65 percent chance of a magnitude 7.0 or larger quake striking the region before 2030. It shouldn't cancel a trip, but it is worth knowing where your hotel's stairwells are.
destinations.what_great: The sheer concentration of history is unmatched, you can walk from a 6th-century Byzantine cathedral to a 17th-century Ottoman mosque to a 15th-century sultan's palace in under twenty minutes, all sitting on the same peninsula where Europe meets Asia. The food scene runs from three-lira simit carts to genuinely excellent seafood on the Bosphorus, and the ferry rides across the strait remain one of the great cheap thrills in world travel, all included on the same Istanbulkart you use for the metro.
destinations.what_ruined: The gap between what Istanbul used to cost and what it costs now catches a lot of travelers off guard, hotel and restaurant prices have risen over 40 percent year on year by some measures, and the major museums now charge foreign-visitor-only prices that can hit 55 euros a head. Layer on well-documented airport taxi scams targeting exactly the tourists who just landed and don't know the going rate, mosque visiting hours that don't accommodate a tight itinerary, and background anxiety about a fault line the city sits directly on top of, and the trip demands more logistics planning than its reputation as an easy long weekend suggests.
tips: Buy an Istanbulkart (130 lira for the card) rather than paying cash fares; a single ride starts at 27 lira and each transfer within the window drops to 19.33, then 14.67, then as low as 9.27 lira.
Hagia Sophia charges foreign visitors 25 euros for the upper gallery area, a fee in place since January 2024; children under 8 enter free with ID.
Topkapi Palace's combined Palace, Harem, and Hagia Irene ticket runs 2,750 lira (about 55 euros) at the gate; it's closed Tuesdays and last entry is 16:30.

The Blue Mosque is free with no ticket needed, but it closes to visitors roughly five times a day for prayer and until about 14:30 on Fridays, and dress code (shoulders and knees covered, headscarf for women) is enforced, so bring your own scarf rather than relying on the communal ones at the door.

From Istanbul Airport (IST), the HAVAIST shuttle bus runs about 275 lira one way and is card or app only, cash is no longer accepted; from Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), HAVABUS to Taksim is about 440 lira cash (roughly 100 lira more by card) and takes about 90 minutes.

Only take taxis from the official marked ranks, confirm the meter is running before you move, and use an app like BiTaksi to lock in the route; a common airport scam is a driver claiming the card machine is broken to force a cash payment at an inflated rate.

Check your visa status before booking: US, Canadian, and Australian citizens (among others) need an e-Visa, about 50 dollars, only through the official evisa.gov.tr site, while EU, UK, and Japanese passport holders currently enter visa-free for 90 days.

Visit March to May or September to November for the best mix of mild weather and manageable crowds; August is the hottest and busiest month, while December through February is the cheapest but brings cold, rain, and occasional snow.

guide.title: Istanbul travel guide 2026: airports, transit, neighborhoods, and mosque rules explained
guide.summary: A practical rundown of how to actually move through Istanbul in 2026, from choosing the right airport transfer to picking a base neighborhood to not offending anyone at the mosque.
guide.body:
Istanbul has two airports and picking the wrong one changes your day. Istanbul Airport (IST) on the European side is the main international hub and where most long-haul flights land; the HAVAIST shuttle bus network connects it to the city for about 275 lira one way, card or app only since cash was phased out, though there's no longer a direct HAVAIST line straight into Sultanahmet, you connect via the HVL-1 route to Beyazıt-Aksaray and pick up the T1 tram. Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) on the Asian side handles a large share of budget and regional carriers; the HAVABUS to Taksim costs about 440 lira in cash (card payment adds roughly a 100 lira surcharge) and takes about 90 minutes, so factor that into any tight connection.

Once you're in the city, buy an Istanbulkart immediately, it's 130 lira for the card and covers metro, tram, bus, and ferry, with the first ride at 27 lira and each transfer within the transfer window getting progressively cheaper, down to about 9.27 lira. The ferries in particular are worth using for their own sake, not just as transport, the crossing between the European and Asian sides past the Bosphorus waterfront is one of the best cheap experiences the city offers and it's covered by the same card as the bus.

Where you stay matters more here than in most cities because the historic peninsula, modern nightlife district, and Asian-side neighborhoods each offer a genuinely different trip. Sultanahmet puts you within walking distance of Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, and Topkapi Palace, which is convenient for a first visit but means tour groups and touts outside your hotel door from morning to night. Beyoğlu and Karaköy, across the Golden Horn, put you closer to the restaurant and nightlife scene along Istiklal Street and the waterfront, with a livelier but louder base. Kadıköy, on the Asian side, is quieter, more residential, and popular with travelers who want a local feel and don't mind a ferry ride to reach the major sights.

Mosque etiquette is not optional and gets enforced at the door. At the Blue Mosque and other active mosques, women need their hair, neck, and shoulders covered and legs covered to below the knee, and men need to avoid shorts above the knee; shoes come off before entering. Free scarves and wraps are available at the entrance but they're shared and not always clean, so bringing a lightweight scarf and covering layer of your own is more comfortable. Remember mosques close to visitors around five times a day for prayer, with Fridays closed until roughly 14:30, so check timing before you build it into a tight itinerary.

On money, card acceptance is widespread in restaurants, shops, and hotels, but carrying some lira in cash is still useful for the HAVABUS, small vendors, and situations where a driver or shop claims their card machine is down, a known tactic worth being skeptical of rather than an automatic reason to hand over cash. With inflation running high, prices you see quoted in older blog posts or guidebooks are likely to be understated, budget with a buffer rather than trusting a number that's more than a few months old.

rating_rationale.overall: The historical density and food scene genuinely earn a high score, but the friction of scam-prone transport and unpredictable pricing keeps it just below the top tier.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime against tourists is low and the city is walkable, but airport taxi scams are well documented into 2025, and the region carries a scientifically estimated elevated earthquake risk that residents and officials both take seriously.
rating_rationale.value: Transit and street food remain genuinely cheap, but sustained 30-plus percent inflation has pushed hotel, restaurant, and major-museum prices to levels that now rival Western Europe, eroding the value Istanbul used to be known for.

destinations.name: Jaipur
destinations.summary: Jaipur's forts and palaces are stunning, but foreigners pay 3 to 20 times what Indians pay at every monument, and drivers will steer you toward commission gem shops if you let them.
destinations.headline: Jaipur is worth it, but budget for a foreigner tax at every gate and a driver who wants a commission stop
destinations.body:
Jaipur, founded on November 18, 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, is one of the earliest planned cities in modern India and earned UNESCO World Heritage City status on July 6, 2019. The nickname Pink City dates to 1876, when the city was painted terracotta pink to welcome the Prince of Wales, and the old city walls still carry that color today. The monuments are the reason people come, and they deliver: Amber Fort's hilltop ramparts and mirrored Sheesh Mahal, the honeycomb sandstone facade of Hawa Mahal with its 953 small jharokha windows built in 1799 for royal women to watch the street unseen, and the City Palace complex that is still partly home to the Jaipur royal family today.

What catches first-time visitors off guard is the pricing structure. Every major site runs a dual-tier system, Indian nationals and foreign nationals pay different prices, and the gap is large. Amber Fort charges Indian adults roughly 100 rupees against 500 rupees for foreign adults, with an even bigger gap for students. City Palace is steeper still, around 400 rupees for Indians versus 1200 rupees for foreigners, with a half price rate for children, students, and seniors. Hawa Mahal is the most extreme ratio of the three, about 10 rupees for Indians against 200 rupees for foreigners, a 20x multiple. A composite ticket covering several monuments together runs roughly 300 rupees for Indian adults versus 1000 rupees for foreign adults and stays valid for two days, which is worth buying if you plan to hit more than two sites since it beats paying separately at each gate.

Getting around is where the real friction shows up. Auto-rickshaw drivers commonly propose an all-day hire rate and, according to travel guides, some will suggest a stop at a jewelry or gem shop along the way, sometimes framed casually as grabbing a beer together first. These shops pay commission to the driver, and the sales pitch inside can be aggressive. The standard advice from experienced travelers is to firmly decline any unscheduled shop stop and to agree on an all-in price up front that explicitly covers the driver's time, fuel, and any waiting, rather than negotiating each leg separately. Government emporiums and some guides also work on a roughly 2 percent commission structure tied to what you buy, so a guide's enthusiasm for a particular shop is not always about quality. The Jaipur Metro, which opened June 3, 2015 as India's sixth metro system, is a cheaper and scam-free alternative for point to point trips within its coverage area, with fares generally between 5 and 25 rupees.

Weather matters more here than in most Indian cities because Jaipur sits in a hot semi-arid zone. December through February is mild and the most comfortable window for walking around forts and markets. Summer is brutal, the city has recorded a high of 49.0°C on May 23, 1994, and May and June routinely bring scorching heat that makes midday sightseeing miserable. Monsoon season, mostly July and August, brings the bulk of the city's roughly 625mm of annual rainfall in short, heavy bursts. On air quality, Jaipur was ranked 33rd among India's larger National Clean Air Cities in a national ranking, a middling result that suggests noticeably worse air than Western tourists are used to, particularly in the cooler months when North Indian cities generally see their air quality decline, though it is not in the same league as Delhi's worst winter smog days. Entry to India requires a visa for most foreign nationals; the e-Tourist visa runs about 10 dollars for a 30-day visa in the April to June window or 25 dollars from July to March, with longer 1-year (40 dollars) and 5-year (200 dollars) options allowing stays of up to 180 days per year.
destinations.what_great:
The monuments themselves earn the hype. Amber Fort's scale and the mirror-work inside the Sheesh Mahal, Hawa Mahal's honeycomb facade of 953 jharokha windows built in 1799, and a City Palace that is still an active royal residence give Jaipur a density of genuinely impressive sights that few cities can match. The Pink City's old walled core, painted that color originally for an 1876 royal visit, is walkable and photogenic, and the Jaipur Metro offers a cheap, hassle-free way to cover ground without negotiating with a driver.

Costs are still low by Western standards even with the foreigner pricing tier, especially food, metro fares of 5 to 25 rupees, and the composite monument ticket if you plan your sightseeing to use it across two days. December through February weather is genuinely pleasant for a full day of walking between sites.
destinations.what_ruined:
The dual pricing system is the single biggest friction point. Foreigners pay roughly 5x at Amber Fort, 3x at City Palace, and a striking 20x at Hawa Mahal compared to Indian nationals, and there is no way around it since it is checked by ID at the gate. Auto-rickshaw and taxi drivers commonly try to route tourists through commission gem and jewelry shops, sometimes with a casual social pretext like inviting you for a drink first, and refusing these detours takes a firm no, repeated more than once in some cases.

Summer heat is a real constraint, with Jaipur having recorded temperatures as high as 49.0°C in late May historically, which effectively rules out comfortable outdoor sightseeing for weeks at a time. Air quality is also a genuine downgrade from what most Western visitors are used to, Jaipur placed only 33rd in a national clean air city ranking, and the e-visa process, while not expensive, is a mandatory extra planning step and cost most travelers to nearby regions do not have to budget for.
tips: Buy the composite ticket if you are visiting more than two monuments: it runs about 300 rupees for Indian adults versus 1000 rupees for foreign adults and stays valid for two days, which beats paying the individual foreigner rate at each gate.

Agree an all-in price with your auto-rickshaw or taxi driver before you leave, covering their time, fuel, and any waiting, and firmly decline any suggested stop at a gem, jewelry, or emporium shop along the way since these pay the driver a commission.

Apply for the e-Tourist visa in advance: a 30-day visa costs about 10 dollars from April to June or 25 dollars from July to March, while 1-year (40 dollars) and 5-year (200 dollars) options allow stays of up to 180 days per year if you plan to return.

Visit between December and February for the most comfortable weather; Jaipur has recorded highs of 49.0°C in late May, and the monsoon in July and August brings the bulk of the city's roughly 625mm of annual rain in short heavy bursts.

Use the Jaipur Metro (fares roughly 5 to 25 rupees) for point-to-point trips within its coverage area instead of negotiating with a rickshaw driver every time, and carry a student ID if you have one since several monuments offer a separate, cheaper student rate.

guide.title: Jaipur Practical Guide: Tickets, Transport, and Timing
guide.summary: A practical rundown of what it actually costs and takes to see Jaipur's forts and palaces without overpaying or getting steered into a commission shop.
guide.body:
Jaipur's must-see list is Amber Fort, City Palace, and Hawa Mahal, and all three use a two-tier pricing system where Indian nationals pay a fraction of what foreign visitors pay. Amber Fort runs roughly 100 rupees for Indian adults against 500 rupees for foreign adults, City Palace is about 400 rupees versus 1200 rupees, and Hawa Mahal is the widest gap at roughly 10 rupees versus 200 rupees. If your itinerary covers more than two sites, the composite ticket, about 300 rupees for Indian adults or 1000 rupees for foreign adults and valid across two days, is the better deal. Bring a student ID if you have one, since most sites also offer a discounted student rate on top of the base tiers.

Getting around the city, the Jaipur Metro opened in June 2015 as India's sixth metro system and charges fares generally between 5 and 25 rupees, making it the cheapest and most scam-free way to move between stops on its line. For everywhere else, auto-rickshaws are the default, and the standard local advice is to negotiate one all-in price for a driver's time, fuel, and parking before you get in rather than paying per stop, and to firmly refuse any detour to a jewelry, gem, or carpet shop a driver suggests, since these operate on a commission system that has nothing to do with quality or price. The same commission dynamic applies to some tour guides at government emporiums.

On timing, aim for December through February, when daytime temperatures are mild and comfortable for a full day of walking. Avoid May and June if you can, historical highs have reached 49.0°C, and the July to August monsoon brings heavy, concentrated rainfall rather than the steady drizzle some travelers expect. Foreign nationals need a visa to enter India; the e-Tourist visa is the standard route, priced around 10 dollars for a 30-day visa from April to June, 25 dollars from July to March, or 40 to 200 dollars for the 1-year and 5-year options respectively, both of which cap stays at 180 days per year. Apply online in advance rather than assuming visa-on-arrival is available, since eligibility varies by nationality.

rating_rationale.overall: World-class, UNESCO-recognized monuments and a walkable historic core make Jaipur a strong destination despite the friction, hence 4 rather than 5.
rating_rationale.safety: Generally safe for tourists during the day but documented gem shop and commission scams, plus advice that solo women should avoid deserted streets outside business hours, keep this at a middling 3.
rating_rationale.value: Costs are low overall, but the foreigner-vs-local pricing gap at every monument (up to 20x at Hawa Mahal) and the added e-visa cost pull this down from a top score.

destinations.name: Kathmandu
destinations.summary: The gateway to the Himalaya, and repeatedly ranked among the most polluted cities on earth in exactly the months most trekkers pass through it.
destinations.headline: Kathmandu in 2026: world's most polluted major city on some mornings, and the permits above it got far more expensive
destinations.body: Kathmandu is a city of 856,767 people at roughly 1,400 metres, in a bowl-shaped valley holding around four million. It is the entry point for essentially all Nepal tourism, and Nepal took 1,158,459 international arrivals in 2025, about 97 percent of the pre-pandemic 2019 level, led by India with 292,438 visitors (25.2 percent), then the United States with 112,316 (9.7 percent), China with 95,480 (8.2 percent), the United Kingdom with 58,684 (5.1 percent) and Bangladesh with 57,545 (5.0 percent). The valley's cultural density is genuine and UNESCO-recognised: Kathmandu Durbar Square, the Swayambhu Mahachaitya, Boudhanath and Pashupatinath are all here, within a short drive of each other. The problem you cannot design around is the air. Kathmandu's topography is a bowl that traps pollution whenever the weather goes calm, and IQAir has repeatedly listed it among the world's ten most polluted major cities through 2026, including February 12 and April 22, 2026, and on March 8, 2026 it ranked as the single most polluted major city in the world, with AQI over 200, classified very unhealthy and dominated by PM2.5. This is not a freak event. The worst readings run January through May and again in November and December, driven by the winter inversion plus forest fires, stubble burning, waste burning and brick kilns in the March-to-May window. Back in 2013 Kathmandu's PM2.5 was measured at 49 micrograms per cubic metre, 4.9 times the WHO recommendation, and a November 2019 report attributed 9,943 annual premature deaths in the city to air pollution. October and November are traditionally the trekking high season for a reason, and the monsoon, with 65 percent of annual precipitation falling June through September, washes the air but closes the mountain views. The other 2026 change is upstream, on the peaks people come here to reach. Nepal raised the Everest climbing royalty for the standard south route in the March-to-May spring season from $11,000 to $15,000, with autumn going from $5,500 to $7,500 and winter and monsoon from $2,750 to $3,750, alongside a mandatory Nepali guide on every expedition, a $4,000 waste management fee and proof of body-repatriation insurance. The stated aim was to cut pollution and crowding, but Nepal still issued a record 492 Everest permits for the 2026 season, and that season had already claimed five lives, three on Everest and one each on Makalu and Makalu II. For ordinary trekkers rather than climbers, the fees remain modest: the Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality permit is NPR 3,000, roughly $23, for the first four weeks, and Sagarmatha National Park entry is NPR 3,000 plus 13 percent VAT, around $28.
destinations.what_great:
Very few cities put this much living religious architecture inside one valley. Kathmandu Durbar Square, the Swayambhu Mahachaitya, Boudhanath and Pashupatinath are all UNESCO-recognised and all still functioning places of worship rather than museums, and you can reasonably see them across a couple of days without leaving the valley. Boudhanath at dusk, with pilgrims circling the stupa, is one of the genuine great sights in Asia.

It is also the most cost-effective adventure hub on the continent. Nepal drew 1,158,459 international visitors in 2025 and the infrastructure that supports them, guides, gear shops in Thamel, domestic flights, permit offices, is concentrated and cheap. Ordinary trekking permits stay modest, with the Khumbu municipality permit around $23 and Sagarmatha National Park entry around $28, so the mountains themselves remain accessible even as the headline climbing fees have soared.
destinations.what_ruined:
The air, plainly. Kathmandu sits in a bowl that traps pollution, and IQAir put it among the world's ten most polluted major cities repeatedly through 2026, including on February 12 and April 22, and ranked it the single most polluted major city in the world on March 8, 2026, with AQI over 200 in the very unhealthy band. The bad season is long, January through May plus November and December, driven by winter inversion and then by forest fires, stubble burning, waste burning and brick kilns from March to May. Historical context makes it worse rather than better: PM2.5 measured 49 micrograms per cubic metre in 2013, 4.9 times the WHO guideline, and a 2019 report tied 9,943 annual premature deaths in the city to air pollution. If you have asthma or are travelling with children, this is a planning constraint, not a footnote.

Above the city, the mountaineering economics have changed sharply. Nepal raised the spring Everest royalty from $11,000 to $15,000, autumn from $5,500 to $7,500 and winter and monsoon from $2,750 to $3,750, added a mandatory Nepali guide, a $4,000 waste management fee and mandatory body-repatriation insurance, all justified as pollution and safety measures, and then issued a record 492 Everest permits for 2026 anyway. Five people had already died in that season, three on Everest and one each on Makalu and Makalu II. Higher prices have not produced fewer people on the mountain.
tips: Check the AQI before you commit to dates. IQAir ranked Kathmandu the world's most polluted major city on March 8, 2026 with AQI over 200, and among the top ten on February 12 and April 22, 2026.

Avoid January through May and November to December if air quality matters to you. Those are Kathmandu's worst months, driven by winter inversion and then fires, stubble and waste burning and brick kilns.
Bring a proper N95-class mask, not a cloth one. PM2.5 is the dominant pollutant, and it was measured at 4.9 times the WHO guideline as far back as 2013.

Budget separately if you are climbing rather than trekking. Nepal's spring Everest royalty rose from $11,000 to $15,000, plus a $4,000 waste management fee, a mandatory Nepali guide and body-repatriation insurance.

Ordinary trekking is still cheap: the Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality permit is NPR 3,000 (about $23) for the first four weeks and Sagarmatha National Park entry is NPR 3,000 plus 13 percent VAT (about $28).

guide.title: Kathmandu Travel Guide: Air Quality, Permits and Season in 2026
guide.summary: How to time a Kathmandu trip around the valley's pollution seasons and the monsoon, and what Nepal's 2026 permit changes actually cost trekkers versus climbers.
guide.body:
Kathmandu sits at about 1,400 metres in a bowl-shaped valley, and that shape is the reason air quality dominates any honest planning conversation. When the weather goes calm, the bowl traps pollution. IQAir listed Kathmandu among the world's ten most polluted major cities on February 12 and April 22, 2026, and ranked it the single most polluted major city in the world on March 8, 2026, with AQI over 200 in the very unhealthy band and PM2.5 the dominant pollutant. The bad stretch runs January through May and again in November and December, worsened between March and May by forest fires, stubble burning, waste burning and brick kilns. This has a long history: PM2.5 measured 49 micrograms per cubic metre in 2013, 4.9 times the WHO recommendation, and a November 2019 report attributed 9,943 annual premature deaths in the city to air pollution. Bring an N95-class mask, check a live AQI reading before booking, and if you have a respiratory condition treat the winter and spring months as a genuine contraindication rather than an inconvenience.

Season works against you in the other direction too. About 65 percent of the valley's annual precipitation falls in the monsoon months of June to September. Monsoon air is clean and the valley is green, but mountain views close in and landslides disrupt road routes. That leaves late September through early November as the classic window: clear air after the rains, open views, and the traditional trekking high season, which is also the busiest and priciest.

On permits, distinguish clearly between trekking and climbing, because the 2026 changes hit only the second. For trekkers heading into the Everest region, the Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality permit costs NPR 3,000, roughly $23, covering the first four weeks, and Sagarmatha National Park entry is NPR 3,000 plus 13 percent VAT, about $28. Those are unchanged in substance and still cheap. For climbers, Nepal raised the Everest royalty on the standard south route from $11,000 to $15,000 for the March-to-May spring season, from $5,500 to $7,500 for autumn and from $2,750 to $3,750 for winter and monsoon, and added a mandatory Nepali guide on every expedition, a $4,000 waste management fee and proof of body-repatriation insurance. The stated purpose was cutting pollution and crowding; the outcome so far is that Nepal issued a record 492 Everest permits for 2026, a season that had already seen five deaths, three on Everest and one each on Makalu and Makalu II. In the valley itself, the sights are close together: Kathmandu Durbar Square, the Swayambhu Mahachaitya, Boudhanath and Pashupatinath are all UNESCO-recognised and all reachable within a day or two of each other, which makes a short acclimatisation stopover here worth building into any trekking itinerary.

rating_rationale.overall: An extraordinary concentration of living UNESCO-listed religious architecture and the best-value adventure base in Asia, marked down hard for air quality that repeatedly ranks among the worst on earth for roughly half the year.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime against visitors is uncommon, but the environmental and infrastructure risks are real: AQI over 200 in the very unhealthy band on bad days, chaotic road traffic, monsoon landslides with 65 percent of annual rain falling June to September, and a seismically active region.
rating_rationale.value: One of the cheapest capitals in Asia for food, lodging and guiding, with ordinary trekking permits still modest at roughly $23 for the Khumbu municipality permit and $28 for Sagarmatha National Park entry; the cost explosion is confined to peak climbing royalties.
