destinations.name: New York City
destinations.summary: NYC delivers world class energy and culture but nickels and dimes you constantly, from $9 congestion tolls to $70 airport taxis and a tipping culture that catches visitors off guard.
destinations.headline: New York City in 2026: incredible city, expensive friction at every turn
destinations.body:
New York City still earns its reputation as one of the world's great cities, but 2026 visitors are navigating a denser layer of fees, tolls, and price hikes than in years past. The biggest structural change is congestion pricing, which launched January 5, 2025, and as of 2026 charges passenger vehicles with E-ZPass $9 to drive into Manhattan below 60th Street during peak hours (5am to 9pm weekdays, 9am to 9pm weekends), dropping to $2.25 overnight. A federal challenge to the program was rejected in March 2026 when a US District Judge ruled in the MTA's favor, so the toll is staying, and it is scheduled to climb to $12 in 2028 and $15 by 2031. Most visitors will not drive, but it affects taxi and rideshare surcharges and overall traffic.

Getting around by subway got a bit pricier too. The base fare rose from $2.90 to $3.00 on January 4, 2026, and single ride paper tickets now cost $3.50. The physical MetroCard is being phased out in favor of OMNY, the tap to pay system, and a new physical OMNY card carries a $2 issuance fee if you want one instead of tapping a bank card or phone. The upside is a weekly fare cap, once you have paid for 12 rides in a rolling seven day period your subway and local bus trips are free for the rest of that week, which caps a heavy user's weekly cost at $35.

Broadway remains one of the city's best values if you play it right. The TKTS discount booth on the red steps in Times Square sells same day tickets, and next day matinees, at 20 to 50 percent off face value, though every ticket carries a flat $8 service charge on top. Expect final prices somewhere between roughly $50 and $150 depending on the show and discount tier, and know that inventory changes daily and lines can be long.

Hotels are where New York really tests a budget. Mid-range Manhattan hotels commonly run $250 to $400 a night, and citywide averages that include outer boroughs land lower, with some trackers reporting a median closer to $156. Whatever rate you book, add roughly 14.75 percent in combined state and city hotel taxes plus a flat $3.50 per night in occupancy fees, a combination that surprises a lot of first time visitors when they see the final folio.

Tipping culture remains a genuine source of friction for international travelers. Surveys have found that 79 percent of foreign visitors feel more pressure to tip in the US than at home, and about half feel scrutinized while doing it. Digital payment screens at coffee shops and counter service spots increasingly prompt for 20, 25, or even 30 percent gratuities before you have even received anything, a habit that is uncommon almost everywhere else in the world and worth budgeting for in advance.

On safety, the data and the perception do not match. Subway crime fell to its lowest level in 16 years through 2025, major transit crime dropped roughly 5 percent year over year, and transit robberies hit the lowest levels ever recorded, yet only about 22 percent of riders say they feel safe on the subway at night even though the MTA's own fall 2025 rider survey put that figure at 63 percent. The core visitor areas, Midtown, the Upper West Side, the Upper East Side, Chelsea, Flatiron, and Lower Manhattan, are consistently low risk, while tourist-targeted theft concentrates around Times Square, Herald Square, and a small number of subway stations during rush hour.

Getting from the airports adds its own cost calculus. JFK's yellow cab flat rate to Manhattan is $70 before tolls and tip, which realistically pushes the total to $90 to $105. The cheaper route is the AirTrain, about $8.75, connected to the subway for another $3.00. LaGuardia has no flat rate at all, so cabs run metered, typically $40 to $70 before tolls and tip since it sits closer to Manhattan.
destinations.what_great:
The subway genuinely is safer than it has been in years, with major transit crime at its lowest point since 2009 and transit robberies at record lows, and the tourist core neighborhoods, Midtown, the Upper West Side, the Upper East Side, Chelsea, Flatiron, and Lower Manhattan, stay consistently low risk. Broadway is still reachable on a budget through the TKTS booth, where same day and next day tickets run 20 to 50 percent off face value, and the weekly OMNY fare cap means heavy subway users stop paying once they have covered 12 rides in seven days, capping the cost at $35 a week.

The sheer density of world class museums, restaurants, and neighborhoods within a single subway system is still unmatched, and the congestion pricing zone has measurably reduced Manhattan traffic since it launched in January 2025, which makes crossing Midtown on foot or by bus noticeably less chaotic than it used to be.
destinations.what_ruined:
Costs stack up fast and often invisibly. A hotel room advertised at $250 a night actually lands closer to $290 once you add roughly 14.75 percent in combined taxes plus the flat $3.50 nightly occupancy fee. Driving into Manhattan below 60th Street now costs $9 during the day under congestion pricing, a toll that is legally settled after a March 2026 court ruling and is scheduled to rise to $12 in 2028 and $15 by 2031. A JFK taxi's advertised $70 flat rate routinely becomes $90 to $105 once tolls and tip are added, and LaGuardia does not even offer a flat rate, leaving visitors guessing at a metered fare.

Tipping is a persistent irritant for international visitors, with surveys showing 79 percent feel more tipping pressure in the US than at home and nearly half feeling judged while doing it, made worse by payment terminals that now default to prompting 20 to 30 percent gratuities at counter service spots where tipping barely existed a decade ago. And while the safety data has genuinely improved, the gap between that data and how safe riders actually feel, only 22 percent report feeling safe on the subway at night despite record low transit robbery numbers, means many visitors will still white knuckle a perfectly safe train ride.
tips: Skip the paper MetroCard, which is being phased out in 2026, and tap in with OMNY directly from a bank card or phone; the base subway fare is $3.00 and rides are free once you have paid for 12 in a rolling seven day period, capping your weekly cost at $35.

Line up early at the TKTS booth on the red steps in Times Square for same day Broadway tickets at 20 to 50 percent off face value, but budget for the flat $8 per ticket service charge added at checkout.

If you are driving into Manhattan below 60th Street, plan for the $9 congestion toll during peak hours (5am to 9pm weekdays, 9am to 9pm weekends) with E-ZPass, or $2.25 overnight; a March 2026 court ruling upheld the program and it is scheduled to rise to $12 in 2028.

From JFK, skip the $70 flat rate taxi (really $90 to $105 with tolls and tip) and take the AirTrain for about $8.75 plus a $3.00 subway ride instead; LaGuardia has no flat taxi rate at all, so expect a metered fare of roughly $40 to $70 before tolls and tip.

Build tipping into your budget everywhere, not just restaurants; digital payment screens at coffee shops and counter service spots now commonly prompt for 20 to 30 percent, a habit that catches most international visitors off guard.
Book Statue of Liberty ferry tickets ahead of time, the base fare is $25.50 for adults and adding pedestal or crown access only costs $0.30 more, but same day slots do sell out.

guide.title: New York City Practical Guide: Getting Around, Costs, and When to Go
guide.summary: A practical rundown of NYC transit, seasonal pricing swings, and the neighborhoods that actually work for a first time visitor in 2026.
guide.body:
Getting around is almost entirely a subway and walking exercise for most visitors, and it works well now that OMNY tap to pay has effectively replaced the MetroCard, with a $3.00 base fare and a weekly cap of $35 once you have paid for 12 rides in seven days. Stick to the numbered and lettered lines that run through Midtown, Lower Manhattan, and Brooklyn's closer neighborhoods, and avoid renting a car entirely since congestion pricing now charges $9 to drive into Manhattan below 60th Street during the day, a toll upheld by a federal court in March 2026 and one that only gets more expensive in coming years.

Season matters more for price than for weather tolerance. Hotel rates in Manhattan swing hard, dropping an estimated 30 to 50 percent during off season windows like late January through February and late November, compared to peak spring and holiday pricing that regularly pushes mid-range rooms toward $400 a night. If your dates are flexible, shifting a trip into a shoulder season is the single biggest lever available for cutting the cost of a New York trip, since taxes of roughly 14.75 percent plus flat nightly fees apply regardless of the room rate.

For neighborhoods, the visitor core, Midtown, the Upper West Side, the Upper East Side, Chelsea, Flatiron, and Lower Manhattan, offers the best mix of safety, walkability, and proximity to major sights, while areas like DUMBO in Brooklyn are worth a dedicated afternoon rather than a home base. Times Square and Herald Square are must sees but are also where petty theft targeting tourists concentrates, so keep bags zipped and phones secured in crowds there specifically.

On money saving moves beyond timing, use the TKTS booth for Broadway rather than paying full price online, ride the free Staten Island Ferry for skyline and Statue of Liberty views instead of a paid cruise if a photo stop is all you need, and compare the Empire State Building's roughly $44 base Main Deck ticket against the pricier $79 combined Main and Top Deck option before assuming you need both. For the airports, factor AirTrain plus subway against a taxi's advertised flat rate, since the real out the door taxi cost from JFK routinely lands $20 to $35 above the quoted $70 once tolls and tip are included.

rating_rationale.overall: Unmatched culture and improving subway safety, but 2026 pricing across hotels, tolls, and transit fees makes it a heavier lift than a few years ago.
rating_rationale.safety: Transit crime is at multi-decade lows and tourist core neighborhoods are consistently low risk, but crime remains concentrated at specific stations and outer areas, so awareness still matters.
rating_rationale.value: Mid-range Manhattan hotels run $250 to $400 a night before roughly 14.75 percent in taxes plus flat nightly fees, and a $9 congestion toll, $70 airport taxi flat rate, and default 20 to 30 percent tip prompts add up fast.

destinations.name: Oaxaca
destinations.summary: Colonial capital and Zapotec heartland in southern Mexico, known for mezcal, mole, Monte Alban, and two festival peaks that overwhelm the city's capacity.
destinations.headline: Oaxaca Review: World-Class Food and Ruins, Priced and Crowded to the Limit in Festival Season
destinations.body:
Oaxaca de Juarez is the capital of Oaxaca state in southern Mexico, and the city centre together with the archaeological site of Monte Alban was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987. The grid of the Centro Historico is Spanish colonial town planning built low and heavy for an earthquake zone, anchored by the Zocalo, the pedestrian Andador Macedonio Alcala, and the Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzman. The former convent beside the church holds the Museo de las Culturas de Oaxaca, which INAH lists at 210 pesos general admission and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, open Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00 and Sunday 10:00 to 15:30, closed Mondays.

Monte Alban itself sits on a levelled ridge about 10 kilometres from the centre and is open daily 8:00 to 17:00 with last admission at 16:00. INAH's official rate is 210 pesos for general admission and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, under the national fee schedule effective January 1, 2026. Sundays are free for Mexicans and legal residents, which also makes Sunday the most crowded day. Mitla, about 45 kilometres southeast and famous for its geometric stone fretwork, is listed by INAH at 210 pesos general admission, 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, with hours of 8:00 to 17:00 and last access at 16:30.

The Centro Historico carries the museums, the Zocalo and the highest prices. Jalatlaco, a few blocks northeast, is the quieter cobbled quarter with murals and smaller kitchens. Xochimilco, uphill to the north, is residential and calm. Reforma is where longer stay visitors and remote workers concentrate.

Arrival is through Oaxaca International Airport, roughly nine kilometres south of the centre. The official airport colectivo runs 135 pesos to Zone 1 covering the Centro Historico and 210 pesos to Zone 2, while a taxi especial is 490 pesos to Zone 1 and more to Zone 2, with rates posted at the terminal booth. Uber and DiDi remain effectively banned across Oaxaca state as of 2026, so ride hailing is not the fallback it is elsewhere in Mexico.

The calendar is unusually consequential. The dry season runs roughly October to April and the rains fall May to September as afternoon downpours, with June the wettest month. Two events dominate. The Guelaguetza culminates on the Lunes del Cerro at the Auditorio Guelaguetza on Cerro del Fortin, falling on Monday July 20 and Monday July 27 in 2026, with reported prices of 1,476 pesos presale and 1,632 pesos regular for Palco A and 1,166 presale and 1,321 regular for Palco B, while Palcos C and D are free on a first arrival basis. Dia de Muertos runs October 31 to November 2, with the vigils at the Santa Cruz Xoxocotlan cemetery about five kilometres from the centre drawing the largest crowds.

Both peaks come with a real cost. Day of the Dead accommodation is reported at 50 to 80 percent above baseline rates with three to five night minimums, and properties commonly sell out by August or September. Tourism to Oaxaca has risen roughly 77 percent since 2020, and residents have organised protests over short term rentals, housing displacement and water allocation, with reports of neighbourhoods going weeks without running water while hotels stayed supplied. Visitors are arriving into an active local dispute, not a neutral backdrop.

The food and mezcal justify the trip on their own. Mercado 20 de Noviembre and Mercado Benito Juarez sit side by side downtown, and the Sunday market at Tlacolula is worth the drive. On mezcal, the honest warning is that cheap tours are the problem: operators charging under about 30 US dollars per person typically recoup the difference through commission on bottle sales, which forces the palenques in and around Santiago Matatlan to hard sell. Paying more for a smaller group that pays the producer properly is the difference between a distillery visit and a sales pitch.
destinations.what_great: Monte Alban is a levelled mountaintop city with 1,500 years of Olmec, Zapotec and Mixtec occupation, open 8:00 to 17:00 for 210 pesos, and it is 10 kilometres from a colonial grid that shares the same 1987 UNESCO inscription. The Museo de las Culturas at Santo Domingo holds the Tomb 7 Mixtec gold. Mercado 20 de Noviembre and the Sunday Tlacolula market are working markets, not displays. Mitla's stone fretwork, 210 pesos general admission, has no equivalent anywhere in Mexico.
destinations.what_ruined: Festival season breaks the city. Day of the Dead lodging is reported at 50 to 80 percent above baseline with three to five night minimums and properties sold out by August. Guelaguetza box seats run to 1,632 pesos. Tourism is up roughly 77 percent since 2020, and residents have protested short-term rentals, displacement and water allocation, with reports of neighbourhoods dry for weeks while hotels stayed supplied. Mezcal tours under 30 dollars recoup costs by pressuring palenques into hard selling. Hierve el Agua closes unpredictably.
tips: Arrive at Monte Alban at the 8:00 opening, since the site closes at 17:00 with last admission at 16:00 and there is almost no shade on the Gran Plaza.
Skip Monte Alban on Sunday if you want space, because free entry for Mexicans and residents that day makes it the most crowded of the week.
Take the official airport colectivo at 135 pesos to the Centro Historico instead of the 490 peso taxi especial, since both are booked at the same posted-rate terminal booth.
Do not plan on Uber or DiDi, which remain effectively banned across Oaxaca state in 2026, and agree a fare with street taxis before getting in.
Buy Guelaguetza tickets only through SuperBoletos, the sole authorised online vendor, or queue for the free Palco C and D seating on the Lunes del Cerro dates of 20 and 27 July 2026.
Carry cash for Hierve el Agua, where entry is cash only at roughly 50 to 70 pesos plus a community fee and there are no ATMs at the site, and confirm within a week that it has not closed.

guide.title: Oaxaca Practical Guide: OAX Transfers, Monte Alban Fees, Festival Months and Real Budgets
guide.summary: Month by month timing around Guelaguetza and Day of the Dead, official airport transfer rates, current INAH site fees, honest daily budget bands, and the scams worth knowing.
guide.body:
Oaxaca has a dry season from roughly October to April and a rainy season from May to September. The rains are afternoon events rather than all day washouts, with most mornings clear, and June is the wettest month. The most comfortable stretch is late January into early March, when the heat has not built and humidity is at its lowest. May, June, September and early October are the cheapest and quietest months, with lower hotel rates and thinner crowds, at the cost of daily afternoon storms. The two dates that will define your trip and your budget are the Guelaguetza, whose Lunes del Cerro performances at the Auditorio Guelaguetza on Cerro del Fortin fall on Monday July 20 and Monday July 27 in 2026, and Dia de Muertos, which runs October 31 to November 2. Both fill the city. Day of the Dead in particular is reported to push accommodation 50 to 80 percent above baseline with three to five night minimums, with many properties sold out by August or September, so book those months ahead or deliberately choose different dates.

Getting in means Oaxaca International Airport, about nine kilometres south of the centre and 20 to 30 minutes by road. The official airport colectivo, a shared van booked at the terminal booth with posted rates, costs 135 pesos to Zone 1, which covers the Centro Historico, and 210 pesos to Zone 2 for outlying neighbourhoods like San Felipe del Agua. A private taxi especial from the same booth is 490 pesos to Zone 1 and costs more to Zone 2, so check the posted board before you pay. Card payment is accepted at the booth. Plan for the absence of ride hailing: Uber and DiDi remain effectively banned across Oaxaca state as of 2026, so street taxis, the colectivo system and walking are the real options.

Getting around the city is overwhelmingly on foot. The Centro Historico grid is compact and the Andador Macedonio Alcala is pedestrianised. For the valley, colectivos and second class buses leave regularly for Mitla, Tlacolula and Santa Maria del Tule, and a hired driver for a full day of valley sites is the efficient alternative to a group tour.

For sites, Monte Alban is the anchor. Open daily 8:00 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:00, admission is 210 pesos general and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents under the INAH schedule that took effect January 1, 2026. Sundays are free for Mexicans and residents, which is exactly why Sunday is the worst day to go for space and quiet. Get there at opening for shade and empty plazas. The Museo de las Culturas de Oaxaca in the former convent at Santo Domingo is 210 pesos general and 105 for nationals and residents, open Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00 and Sunday 10:00 to 15:30, closed Mondays, and the Tomb 7 Mixtec goldwork inside is genuinely world class. Mitla, 45 kilometres southeast, is listed by INAH at 210 pesos general and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, 8:00 to 17:00, last access 16:30, and its geometric stone mosaics are unlike anything else in Mexico. Hierve el Agua, the mineral terraces east of the city, is the one to approach with caution: entry is cash only and typically quoted in the range of 50 to 70 pesos plus a small community fee, but the site has closed unpredictably during an ongoing dispute between the co-managing communities, so confirm access within a week of going. The Sunday market at Tlacolula is worth building a day around. The thing to skip is any bargain mezcal tour priced under about 30 US dollars per person.

On budget, the verifiable line items are the airport transfer at 135 to 490 pesos, Monte Alban at 210 pesos, the Santo Domingo museum at 210 pesos and Mitla at 210 pesos. At roughly 18 pesos to the US dollar, that is about 7 to 27 dollars for the transfer and about 12 dollars for each of the three sites. Building outward from those, a realistic daily total is about 45 to 65 dollars for a budget traveller in a hostel or guesthouse eating at Mercado 20 de Noviembre, about 90 to 150 dollars for a mid range visitor in a Centro boutique hotel with restaurant meals and one valley excursion, and 250 dollars and up during Guelaguetza or Dia de Muertos, when lodging alone can consume the entire mid range figure.

On safety, Oaxaca state carries a US State Department Level 2 advisory, exercise increased caution, which is the same tier as much of the country and well below a do not travel designation. The practical risks in the city are petty theft in crowded markets and around festival crowds, and taxi overcharging, which is best managed by agreeing a fare before getting in since meters are uncommon. Carry cash for Hierve el Agua and rural markets, since there are no ATMs at the terraces. The commission driven mezcal tour is the most common commercial trap. Finally, be aware of the local context: tourism is up roughly 77 percent since 2020 and residents have protested over short term rentals, displacement and water access, so occasional demonstrations and road blockages are a genuine possibility rather than a curiosity.

rating_rationale.overall: The 1987 UNESCO listing pairing the colonial centre with Monte Alban, plus a food and mezcal culture with no real equivalent in Mexico, makes this a first-rank destination in almost any month.
rating_rationale.safety: Oaxaca state sits at a US State Department Level 2 advisory, exercise increased caution, with everyday risk in the city limited mainly to petty theft, taxi overcharging and occasional protest-related road blockages.
rating_rationale.value: Site fees are low at 210 pesos for Monte Alban and 210 pesos for Mitla and the airport colectivo is 135 pesos, but Day of the Dead lodging reportedly runs 50 to 80 percent above baseline with multi-night minimums.

destinations.name: Osaka
destinations.summary: Japan's street-food and nightlife capital, cheap for foreigners because the yen is near 40-year lows, and crowded for exactly the same reason.
destinations.headline: Osaka in 2026: post-Expo, post-cheap-yen-honeymoon, and now taxed for the crowds it invited
destinations.body: Osaka is Japan's third most populous city, with 2,816,247 residents as of October 1, 2025, at the center of a metropolitan region of more than 19 million. It is the less formal, more working-class counterpart to Kyoto an hour away: Osaka Castle dates to 1583, Dotonbori is a canal lined with neon and food stalls, Shinsekai sits under the Tsutenkaku tower, and the city's food culture is summed up by kuidaore, an Edo-era jab that Osakans devour food until they collapse and which the city has long since adopted as a boast. Universal Studios Japan, on the west side, drew 16 million visitors in 2024, making it the most visited theme park in Asia and third in the world. The defining fact of visiting in 2026 is the exchange rate. The yen entered 2026 in the mid-150s per US dollar and broke above 163 on July 21, 2026, its weakest against the dollar in nearly four decades. Against 2019's roughly 110 yen to the dollar, that is a structural discount, and it is the engine behind a record 42.7 million international visitors to Japan in 2025, up 15.8 percent on the previous record of 36.9 million in 2024, with visitor spending hitting a record 9.5 trillion yen. Japan is now projected to receive about 41.4 million foreign visitors in 2026, a roughly 2.8 percent dip and the first annual decline in years. Osaka rode Expo 2025, held at Yumeshima from April to October 2025 with a projected 28 million visitors, and came out of it with roughly 37 billion yen in surplus split among city and prefectural governments. The bill for all this now arrives in fees. Japan tripled its departure tax from 1,000 to 3,000 yen effective July 1, 2026, explicitly citing congestion and nuisance behavior at tourist destinations; the tax is bundled into airline and cruise tickets booked from that date. Osaka Prefecture raised its accommodation tax from September 1, 2025 to 200 yen per person per night for rooms of 5,000 to under 15,000 yen, 400 yen for 15,000 to under 20,000, and 500 yen at 20,000 and above, with rooms under 5,000 yen still exempt, which is why a lot of budget travelers in Dotonbori-area business hotels pay nothing at all. From March 1, 2026, that tax is charged separately from the room rate and must be settled on-site even on prepaid bookings, and licensed minpaku private lodging in Osaka now collects it too. Day-to-day costs remain genuinely low by developed-world standards: Osaka Metro fares start at 190 yen for trips under 3 km with a 820 yen day pass, and Numbeo estimates a single person's monthly costs excluding rent at about 119,506 yen. The crowd picture is uneven rather than uniformly worse. The Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka Golden Route is congested at peak periods, but districts that used to be wall-to-wall Chinese tour groups, including parts of Dotonbori, have reportedly thinned.
destinations.what_great:
Osaka is the best eating city in Japan and it is not especially close. Dotonbori, Kuromon and the neighborhood standing bars deliver takoyaki, okonomiyaki and kushikatsu at prices that still read as cheap to anyone earning in dollars or euros, and the culture around food here is louder, later and less precious than Kyoto's. Osaka Castle, first built in 1583, anchors a genuinely good park, and Shinsekai under the Tsutenkaku tower is the closest thing Japan has to a preserved mid-century entertainment district.

Practically, it works. Osaka Metro fares start at 190 yen with an 820 yen day pass, Kansai International puts you inside a huge international network, and the city sits an hour from Kyoto and Nara, which makes it the sane base for the whole region. Universal Studios Japan pulled 16 million visitors in 2024 as the most visited theme park in Asia, and the yen near four-decade lows means the entire trip costs a foreign visitor meaningfully less than it did in 2019.
destinations.what_ruined:
The discount that brought you here brought everyone else too. Japan took a record 42.7 million international visitors in 2025, up 15.8 percent on 2024's record, and the Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka Golden Route absorbs the bulk of that at peak periods. Governments are now pricing the congestion: the departure tax tripled from 1,000 to 3,000 yen on July 1, 2026, explicitly justified by congestion and nuisance behavior, and Osaka's accommodation tax rose in September 2025 to as much as 500 yen per person per night, now billed separately on-site from March 1, 2026 even when you prepaid.

The other thing to be honest about is that Osaka is a working industrial port city, not a postcard. It is loud, the architecture is mostly postwar concrete, and the famous districts are small: Dotonbori is a couple of crowded blocks, not a neighborhood you spend three days in. Expo 2025 has come and gone, so the once-in-a-generation reason to be here specifically has expired, and Japan's arrivals are projected to dip about 2.8 percent in 2026, the first annual decline in years, which is a sign the surge is normalizing rather than that the crowds are gone.
tips: Book flights before you finalize the budget. Japan's departure tax tripled from 1,000 to 3,000 yen on July 1, 2026, bundled into tickets, though bookings made before that date are exempt from the increase.

Expect the accommodation tax as a separate on-site charge. Since March 1, 2026, Osaka's lodging tax is billed apart from the room rate even on prepaid reservations, at 200 to 500 yen per person per night depending on rate.
Stay in a room under 5,000 yen a night and you pay no accommodation tax at all, which covers a lot of business hotels near Dotonbori.
Get the 820 yen Osaka Metro day pass if you plan more than four rides. Single fares start at 190 yen for trips under 3 km and climb with distance.
Base yourself in Osaka for the region rather than Kyoto. Kyoto and Nara are both easy day trips, and Osaka's rooms and food are cheaper than Kyoto's at every tier.
Skip peak Golden Week and the autumn foliage weeks if crowds bother you. Japan still expects about 41.4 million foreign visitors in 2026 and the Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka corridor takes the brunt.

guide.title: Osaka Travel Guide: Taxes, Transit and Timing in 2026
guide.summary: What Osaka actually costs a foreign visitor in 2026 once the new departure and accommodation taxes are counted, plus how to get around and when to go.
guide.body:
Most visitors arrive through Kansai International, and the first thing worth understanding is the tax layer that was added over the past year. Japan tripled its departure tax from 1,000 to 3,000 yen effective July 1, 2026, citing congestion and nuisance behavior at tourist destinations; it is included in the price of airline and cruise tickets booked on or after that date, while earlier bookings are exempt from the increase. Separately, Osaka Prefecture's accommodation tax has been 200 yen per person per night for rooms priced 5,000 to under 15,000 yen, 400 yen for 15,000 to under 20,000, and 500 yen at 20,000 and up since September 1, 2025, with rooms under 5,000 yen exempt. From March 1, 2026, that tax is charged separately from the room rate and paid on-site even for prepaid reservations, and licensed minpaku private lodgings in Osaka now collect it as well. None of these are large sums individually, but they are the ones travelers get surprised by at check-in.

Getting around is easy and cheap. Osaka Metro fares start at 190 yen for journeys under 3 km, and a day card runs 820 yen, so anything past four rides in a day pays for the pass. The city is compact enough that Dotonbori, Shinsekai and Osaka Castle are all short hops apart, and Kyoto and Nara are both comfortable day trips, which is the main argument for basing yourself here rather than in more expensive Kyoto. Numbeo puts a single person's monthly cost of living in Osaka excluding rent at about 119,506 yen, which is the underlying reason day-to-day spending here feels light to visitors.

On timing, the currency is the story. The yen entered 2026 in the mid-150s per dollar and broke above 163 on July 21, 2026, near its weakest in nearly four decades, against roughly 110 in 2019. That discount drove a record 42.7 million international visitors to Japan in 2025 and record spending of 9.5 trillion yen, and 2026 is projected at about 41.4 million, a roughly 2.8 percent dip and the first annual decline in years. Practically, that means the Golden Route is still busy at peak but slightly less brutal than 2025, and reporting suggests Dotonbori's Chinese tour-group density in particular has thinned. Expo 2025 ran at Yumeshima from April to October 2025 with a projected 28 million visitors and left roughly 37 billion yen in surplus to city and prefectural governments, but it is over, so plan around normal seasonality: avoid Golden Week and the peak autumn foliage weeks, and budget around typhoon risk in late summer.

rating_rationale.overall: Outstanding food, nightlife and regional access at a real currency discount, marked down because the marquee sights are compact, the city is aesthetically plain outside its neon strips, and the Golden Route crowding is real at peak.
rating_rationale.safety: Japan is consistently among the safest countries for travelers, with very low rates of violent crime; the practical risks in Osaka are pickpocketing in packed nightlife districts and typhoon-season weather disruption, not personal safety.
rating_rationale.value: The yen broke above 163 to the dollar in July 2026, near 40-year lows, and Metro rides start at 190 yen with an 820 yen day pass. Marked down one point because the departure tax tripled to 3,000 yen and Osaka's accommodation tax now adds up to 500 yen per person per night.

destinations.name: Paris
destinations.summary: Paris delivers on the postcard, but 2026 brings mandatory timed-entry booking everywhere, a two-tier Louvre price for non-EU visitors, and a metro ticketing system mid-overhaul.
destinations.headline: Paris in 2026: the Louvre now charges non-EU visitors 45% more, and paper metro tickets are being phased out
destinations.body:
Paris earns its reputation, and two years after hosting the 2024 Olympics the city is still cashing in the legacy. The Seine reopened to public swimming after a century-long ban, with three supervised sites at Bras Marie, Bercy and Grenelle that opened on July 5, 2025, following a roughly 1.4 billion euro water-quality cleanup. For summer 2026, Paris is expanding to eleven supervised swimming areas starting July 4. The Olympic Aquatics Centre in Saint-Denis is now a public facility and hosts the 2026 European Swimming Championships, a rare case of Olympic infrastructure actually benefiting locals afterward instead of sitting empty.

The money side is where honesty matters most. As of January 14, 2026, the Louvre introduced a two-tier price: 22 euros for EU/EEA residents and 32 euros for everyone else, a 45 percent jump for non-EU visitors from the old flat rate. Entry is free under 18, for EU residents aged 18 to 25, and on the first Saturday evening of each month from 18:00 to 21:45, but timed-slot booking through ticket.louvre.fr is mandatory for every visitor, free entry included, and slots are released up to 60 days ahead and do sell out in peak season. The Eiffel Tower runs the same logic: stairs to the second floor start around 14.80 euros for an adult, summit access by lift runs up to about 36.70 euros, and lift slots can be booked 60 days out versus 40 days for stairs. If you're doing several paid sites, the Paris Museum Pass runs 85 euros for two days, 105 for four, or 125 for six, covering 50-plus attractions including Versailles, Orsay and the Arc de Triomphe, though nine of the biggest names, including the Louvre and Orsay, still require you to book a free timed slot separately even with the pass in hand.

Getting around is in the middle of a real transition. The old paper Ticket t+ was discontinued in 2025 and replaced by a Metro-Train-RER ticket and a separate Bus-Tram ticket, both loaded onto a Navigo card, with a single fare priced at 2.55 euros as of January 1, 2026. A reusable Navigo Easy card costs 2 euros to buy. Remaining magnetic paper tickets stop working on buses in May 2026 and across the entire metro, RER and train network in June 2026, so anyone still carrying old paper stock needs to use it up or switch over. From Charles de Gaulle airport, the RER B into central Paris runs on a dedicated Paris Region-Airports fare priced at 14 euros for an adult as of January 1, 2026, with trains roughly every 6 to 15 minutes and a ride of around 30 to 40 minutes.

The tourist tax adds up fast and is easy to miss when comparing hotel prices online. As of January 1, 2026, Paris raised its taxe de sejour rates and folded in an Ile-de-France Mobilites transport surcharge equal to 200 percent of the base tax, pushing the per-adult, per-night charge to roughly 15.93 euros in a palace or unclassified rental, 11.70 euros at a 5-star, around 8.45 euros at a 4-star, and 5.53 euros at a 3-star. It applies per adult per night and is charged on top of the room rate, not included in it, and children under 18 are exempt. Drivers should also know that since January 1, 2025, only vehicles carrying a Crit'Air 0, 1 or 2 sticker are allowed into the central low-emission zone, with a 68 euro fine for noncompliance, though an exemption for older Crit'Air 3 vehicles has been extended through the end of 2026.

None of this is exotic danger, but the friction is real and repetitive. The petition scam near the Eiffel Tower and the Louvre, where someone posing as deaf or mute pushes a clipboard at you while an accomplice works your pockets, is still active. So is the friendship bracelet trick around Montmartre and Sacre-Coeur, where a stranger ties a bracelet on your wrist before demanding payment for it. Unofficial ticket sellers and people posing as helpful strangers at metro machines are a smaller but persistent nuisance. None of it is violent, all of it is avoidable by not engaging, but tourists who show up expecting a stroll through a museum brochure get caught off guard by how transactional the city has become around its own landmarks.
destinations.what_great:
The Seine swimming reopening is a genuine, verifiable win from the Olympics, not marketing spin. Three supervised sites opened in 2025 and the city is expanding to eleven for summer 2026, alongside a public Olympic Aquatics Centre that now hosts real community swimming instead of sitting fenced off. The city's core appeal, walkable historic neighborhoods, food, and world-class museums, hasn't changed, and options like the Paris Museum Pass make it possible to see a lot for a fixed, predictable cost if you plan the reservations.

Transit remains cheap by major-city standards even after the 2026 fare update, at 2.55 euros a ride, and the RER B gives a fast, direct link from Charles de Gaulle without needing a taxi or rideshare. For travelers willing to book ahead, timed entry actually means shorter lines once you arrive, since crowd flow is capped by design rather than by chance.
destinations.what_ruined:
The friction is all in the fine print. The Louvre's new two-tier pricing, 22 euros for EU/EEA residents versus 32 euros for everyone else since January 14, 2026, is a real cost difference many non-EU visitors won't see coming until they're at checkout. Mandatory timed-entry booking at the Louvre and Eiffel Tower means spontaneous visits are largely dead, walk-ups risk being turned away when slots are full, and the booking windows (60 days for most, 40 for Eiffel Tower stairs) require actual pre-trip planning.

The metro ticketing changeover is genuinely confusing right now, with paper Ticket t+ discontinued, a new Navigo-based system in place, and old magnetic tickets set to stop working entirely by June 2026, a rolling deadline that trips up visitors using outdated guides. Add a tourist tax that can run close to 16 euros per adult per night on top of the room rate, and persistent low-grade scams (the petition trick, the friendship bracelet con) clustered right at the landmarks you came to see, and the honest picture is a city that rewards research and punishes anyone who shows up assuming it will just work like it used to.
tips: Book Louvre timed-entry slots at ticket.louvre.fr up to 60 days ahead; since January 14, 2026 non-EU visitors pay 32 euros versus 22 euros for EU/EEA residents, and even free entry (under 18, EU residents 18-25) requires a reserved slot.

Buy a reusable Navigo Easy card (2 euros) rather than relying on paper tickets: the old Ticket t+ is discontinued and remaining magnetic paper tickets stop working on buses in May 2026 and across the full metro/RER/train network in June 2026.

For the Eiffel Tower, book the lift up to 60 days out and stairs up to 40 days out on the official site; stairs-to-second-floor starts around 14.80 euros while summit-by-lift runs up to about 36.70 euros for an adult.

Budget for the taxe de sejour separately from your room rate: as of January 1, 2026 it runs up to roughly 15.93 euros per adult per night at palace-tier or unclassified properties, charged per person, per night, with kids under 18 exempt.
From Charles de Gaulle, take the RER B on the dedicated Paris Region-Airports fare (14 euros as of January 1, 2026) rather than a taxi for a roughly 30-40 minute direct ride into the city.

Ignore anyone at the Eiffel Tower, Louvre, or Montmartre/Sacre-Coeur who approaches with a petition to sign or a bracelet to tie on your wrist; both are established scams that end in a demand for money or a distraction for pickpockets.

guide.title: Paris Practical Guide: Getting Around, Booking Ahead, and Not Overpaying in 2026
guide.summary: A practical rundown of Paris logistics for 2026: transit ticketing mid-changeover, mandatory timed entry at major sights, the tourist tax, and where the money-saving moves actually are.
guide.body:
Getting around Paris still centers on the metro, and it remains one of the densest, most walkable-adjacent systems of any major capital, but the ticketing is mid-transition. The old paper Ticket t+ was phased out in 2025 in favor of a Metro-Train-RER ticket and a separate Bus-Tram ticket, both tied to a Navigo card, with a single ride priced at 2.55 euros as of January 1, 2026. Buy a reloadable Navigo Easy card for 2 euros rather than chasing paper stock, since remaining magnetic tickets stop working on buses in May 2026 and across the whole rail network by June 2026. From Charles de Gaulle airport, the RER B runs a dedicated Paris Region-Airports fare at 14 euros for adults and gets you into the city center in roughly 30 to 40 minutes, faster and cheaper than a taxi in most traffic conditions.

On timing, shoulder seasons (spring before late May, and September into October) bring milder crowds and weather than peak summer, when timed-entry slots for the Louvre and Eiffel Tower sell out fastest, particularly around sunset for the Tower's summit. Since major sights now require booked, timed slots rather than walk-up access, the biggest planning move is reserving the Louvre (ticket.louvre.fr, up to 60 days ahead) and Eiffel Tower (official site, 60 days for lift, 40 for stairs) before you leave home, not after you land.

For neighborhoods, the Marais offers dense, walkable history and food without the landmark-adjacent scam pressure of the Eiffel Tower or Sacre-Coeur areas, while Montmartre is worth visiting but requires more vigilance around the friendship bracelet scam near the basilica steps. If you're visiting multiple paid museums, run the math on the Paris Museum Pass (85 euros for two days, 105 for four, 125 for six, covering 50-plus sites) against your specific itinerary, since it only pays off if you're actually hitting several included attractions and you'll still need to book free timed slots at the nine sites, including the Louvre and Orsay, that require them regardless of pass status. Finally, factor the taxe de sejour into your accommodation budget from the start rather than treating it as a checkout surprise: it now runs up to roughly 15.93 euros per adult per night at the top end following the January 2026 rate increase and Ile-de-France Mobilites transport surcharge.

rating_rationale.overall: World-class sights and a genuinely improved Seine/swimming legacy from the Olympics, offset by real planning friction around timed entry and ticketing transition.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime is not the concern; petty scams (petition, friendship bracelet, bogus ticket sellers) clustered at major landmarks are the recurring, verifiable risk.
rating_rationale.value: Base transit is still cheap at 2.55 euros a ride, but the new non-EU Louvre surcharge, summit-level Eiffel Tower pricing, and a tourist tax up to roughly 15.93 euros per adult per night add up quickly.

destinations.name: Petra
destinations.summary: A genuinely staggering Nabataean city carved into rose-red rock, undercut by a two-tier ticket system, punishing midday heat, and persistent donkey and horse touts working the Siq.
destinations.headline: Petra is worth the walk, but the pricing is a maze and the animal touts never stop asking
destinations.body:
Petra was carved and built by the Nabataeans starting around the 4th century BC, who called their capital Raqmu, and by the 2nd century BC it was the seat of a wealthy Nabataean trading kingdom controlling incense and spice routes across Arabia. Rome annexed it in 106 AD as the province of Arabia Petraea, after which the city slowly faded from major trade routes and largely dropped out of Western knowledge until Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt talked his way in disguised as a Muslim traveler in 1812. UNESCO listed Petra as a World Heritage Site on December 6, 1985, and in 2007 it was voted one of the New7Wonders of the World, cementing its place as Jordan's single biggest tourism draw.

The approach alone justifies the trip. You walk down the Siq, a narrow sandstone gorge that in places is only 3 to 4 meters wide with walls rising far overhead, before it opens onto Al Khazneh, the Treasury facade, a rock cut monument roughly 24 meters wide and 37 meters tall. That is only the entrance. The wider Petra Archaeological Park covers about 264 square kilometers at an elevation of around 810 meters, and seeing more than the Treasury means real walking, including an approximately 800 step climb to reach the Monastery (Ad Deir), a facade even larger than the Treasury at roughly 45 meters tall and 50 meters wide. There is also a separate, steeper stair route up to the High Place of Sacrifice.

The money side is where the honesty has to kick in. Standard entrance tickets for visitors staying overnight in Jordan run 50 JD for one day, 55 JD for two days, and 60 JD for three days, while same day visitors who are not staying overnight in the country are charged a steep 90 JD. Children under 12 enter free with a parent, and Jordanian university students pay just 1 JD. The Jordan Pass, bought online before arrival, bundles Petra admission with entry to more than 40 other sites nationwide, including Jerash and Wadi Rum, in tiers of 70 JD (1 day Petra), 75 JD (2 day), and 80 JD (3 day), and for travelers staying at least a few nights in Jordan it also waives the standard 40 JD tourist visa fee, which makes it the better deal for almost anyone not on a lightning day trip.

Heat and hydration are a real planning issue, not a throwaway warning. Petra sits in a semi arid zone that gets brutally hot in summer with minimal shade along most trails, so budgeting for bottled water bought inside the park (expect to pay well above outside prices across the day) is standard advice, alongside a hat, sunscreen, and good shoes for uneven ancient stone. Winter visits, by contrast, can mean cold mornings requiring a coat, hat, and gloves. Visitor numbers had climbed to nearly 1.2 million in 2019 before COVID and regional instability cut that to around 905,000 by 2022, and the site took a hit from serious flash flooding in December 2022 that damaged parts of the Siq area.
destinations.what_great:
The Siq to Treasury walk is one of the most theatrical entrances to any archaeological site on earth, and the scale of the carving, a facade roughly 37 meters tall cut directly into sandstone cliff face, holds up to the hype. Push further into the park and the crowds thin fast: the Monastery climb, the High Place of Sacrifice, and the Royal Tombs reward the effort with far fewer people and equally dramatic rock cut architecture. Early entry at opening gives a real shot at photographing the Treasury without a crowd in frame, and the site's UNESCO and New7Wonders status is, for once, earned rather than marketing spin.

The two tier ticket system is annoying but at least transparent once you know it exists, and the Jordan Pass genuinely saves money for anyone spending more than a day or two in the country, since it folds in the visa fee on top of dozens of other site admissions.
destinations.what_ruined:
The pricing structure punishes spontaneity. Show up as a same day visitor without an overnight stay booked in Jordan and the entrance fee jumps to 90 JD, nearly double the overnight rate, which is a steep penalty for travelers doing a quick cross border trip from Israel or Egypt. Bottled water inside the park is marked up heavily, and there is minimal shade on the long walks to the Monastery or High Place of Sacrifice, so a midday summer visit without serious water and sun planning is genuinely risky.

The animal transport touts are the most consistently reported friction point. Horse, donkey, and camel operators press hard for business along the Siq and inside the site, often quoting different prices than what is nominally included in the ticket, and the animals themselves are frequently documented with saddle sores and rough treatment, which is reason enough to walk instead. Tourist police do patrol the main routes, but the pressure to hire an unwanted guide or ride is near constant for first time visitors who have not been warned in advance.
tips: Buy the Jordan Pass online before you fly: it bundles Petra with 40+ other Jordanian sites and, for stays of several nights or more, waives the standard 40 JD tourist visa fee, making it cheaper than paying separately in almost every case.
Avoid entering as a same-day visitor without a Jordan overnight stay if you can help it: that status is charged 90 JD, nearly double the 50 JD overnight-visitor one-day rate.

Budget real money and time for water: the park has minimal shade on the walk to the Monastery or the roughly 800-step climb to the High Place of Sacrifice, and bottled water sold inside costs noticeably more than outside.

Skip the horse, donkey, and camel rides pressed on you along the Siq: welfare concerns around these animals are well documented, the pricing is inconsistently quoted versus what is nominally covered by your ticket, and walking is entirely manageable for most visitors.

Check your government's current Jordan travel advisory before booking: the UK FCDO's 22 July 2026 update flags heightened regional risk near the Syrian border and around Aqaba's airport and seaport following strikes since 8 July 2026, even though it does not cover Petra itself.
Go for opening time if you want the Treasury photo without a crowd of tour groups in frame; the site opens early and fills in steadily through the morning.

guide.title: Petra Travel Guide: Tickets, Timing, and Getting Around
guide.summary: A practical rundown of how to buy in, when to go, and how to move through Petra without overpaying or overheating.
guide.body:
Getting to Petra usually means routing through Amman or Aqaba. From Amman, the JETT bus runs to Petra for around 10 JD one-way and takes roughly 3.5 hours, while local minibuses are cheaper at around 7 JD but slower and less predictable on schedule. From Aqaba on the Red Sea coast, a taxi to Petra runs around 55 JD one-way, which is worth splitting among a group. Many visitors also arrive on organized day tours crossing from Eilat, Israel, though those tend to run in the neighborhood of 220 USD per person once transport, guiding, and the same-day entrance premium are all included, which is significantly more than doing it independently with an overnight stay in Jordan.

On timing, decide upfront whether you are doing Petra as a rushed day trip or an unhurried overnight stop in the nearby town of Wadi Musa. A single day covers the Siq, the Treasury, and the main street of facades and tombs, but it will not comfortably fit the Monastery climb or the High Place of Sacrifice as well. A two-day pass, at 55 JD standalone or 75 JD via Jordan Pass, gives enough slack to split the site into an easier first day and a harder hiking day, and lets you catch both a cooler early morning and a quieter late afternoon session rather than one long slog through midday heat.

Money-wise, the core decision is Jordan Pass versus paying separately. If Petra is one stop among several in Jordan, the Pass essentially always wins once the visa fee waiver is factored in for qualifying stays. If Petra is the only stop on a short cross-border day trip, you are likely stuck paying the higher 90 JD same-day rate regardless, since Pass eligibility and the discounted overnight ticket both assume you are actually staying the night somewhere in Jordan.

For comfort, plan around the season. Summer means real heat with little shade on the longer trails, so carry more water than feels necessary, wear a proper hat, and consider a very early start before the site fills up. Winter, especially December and January, can bring cold mornings that call for a coat, hat, and gloves, a detail that surprises visitors who picture Jordan as uniformly desert-hot year round. Footwear matters throughout: the Siq's floor and the paths up to the Monastery are uneven ancient stone, not paved walkway, so sturdy closed shoes beat sandals.

rating_rationale.overall: A rock cut ancient city that lives up to its reputation architecturally, docked a point for aggressive touting and a punitive same-day ticket price.
rating_rationale.safety: UK FCDO advisory (updated 22 July 2026, current as of 1 August 2026) advises against all travel within 3km of the Jordan-Syria border and against all but essential travel to Aqaba's airport and seaport, citing regional strikes and retaliatory attacks since 8 July 2026 affecting US military and civilian infrastructure in Jordan; Petra itself sits well away from those specific zones but travelers should check the current advisory before finalizing plans.
rating_rationale.value: 50 to 60 JD standard entry (or 90 JD same-day) is expensive for a single site by regional standards, though the Jordan Pass at 70 to 80 JD, which also waives the 40 JD visa fee for longer stays, meaningfully improves the math for most itineraries.

facts_checked: Standard Petra entrance fees for overnight visitors: 50 JD (1 day), 55 JD (2 day), 60 JD (3 day); same-day (non-overnight) visitors pay 90 JD (Wikivoyage)
Children under 12 enter free with parents; Jordanian university students pay 1 JD (Wikivoyage)
Jordan Pass tiers: 70 JD (1 day Petra), 75 JD (2 day), 80 JD (3 day), includes 40+ Jordanian sites and can waive the 40 JD visa fee for qualifying stays (Wikivoyage, JordanPass.jo)
The Siq is a narrow gorge only 3 to 4 meters wide in places leading to the Treasury (Wikipedia)
Al-Khazneh (Treasury) is approximately 24 meters wide and 37 meters tall (Wikipedia)
The Monastery (Ad Deir) is approximately 45 meters tall and 50 meters wide, reached via roughly 800 steps (Wikipedia, Wikivoyage)
Petra Archaeological Park sits at about 810 meters elevation and covers approximately 264 square kilometers (Wikipedia)
Petra was UNESCO World Heritage listed on December 6, 1985, and named a New7Wonders of the World site in 2007 (Wikipedia)
Petra was founded/settled by the Nabataeans; Rome annexed it in 106 AD as Arabia Petraea; Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt rediscovered it for the West in 1812 (Wikipedia)
Petra visitor numbers were nearly 1.2 million in 2019 and around 905,000 in 2022 (Wikipedia)
Petra suffered heavy flooding in December 2022 (Wikipedia)
JETT bus from Amman to Petra costs around 10 JD one-way and takes about 3.5 hours; local minibus is cheaper at around 7 JD; taxi from Aqaba runs around 55 JD one-way (Wikivoyage)
Horse, donkey, and camel touts are a persistent presence at Petra, with documented animal welfare concerns; tourist police patrol the site (Wikivoyage)

UK FCDO Jordan travel advisory, updated 22 July 2026: advises against all travel within 3km of the Jordan-Syria border and against all but essential travel to Aqaba's airport and seaport, citing strikes and retaliatory attacks since 8 July 2026 involving Iran and affecting US military and civilian infrastructure in the region including Jordan

destinations.name: Porto
destinations.summary: A UNESCO-listed river city that is still genuinely cheap to eat in, and is now taxing and licensing its way through the same overtourism squeeze as Lisbon.
destinations.headline: Porto in 2026: the tourist tax went up, the short-term rentals got frozen, and the francesinha is still under 10 euros
destinations.body: Porto is a city of 273,476 people at the mouth of the Douro, inside a metropolitan area of 1,861,727, and its historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. The postcard is real: the Ribeira waterfront, the 172-metre Dom Luis I Bridge opened in 1886, Sao Bento station built between 1900 and 1916 and tiled floor to ceiling, and across the river in Vila Nova de Gaia the port wine lodges that have handled the packaging, transport and export of the fortified wine for centuries. It is also small, steep and concentrated, which is exactly why the tourism numbers now bite. More than 3 million tourists visited in 2025, against 2.8 million overnight visitors plus 1.4 million day-trippers back in 2017, and Francisco Sa Carneiro Airport handled 17 million passengers by 2025. Porto has been named European Best Destination three times, in 2012, 2014 and 2017, and picked up World's Leading Seaside Metropolitan Destination in 2024, and the awards have done what awards do. The policy response in 2026 is two-pronged. The municipal tourist tax rose from around 2 euros to 3 euros per person per night, capped at seven nights, so a maximum of 21 euros per trip, with the revenue earmarked for cultural heritage and infrastructure; Vila Nova de Gaia across the river has raised its own tax as well, which matters because a lot of visitors sleep on the Gaia side. Separately, Portugal has tightened oversight of alojamento local short-term rental registrations, with the Mais Habitacao programme freezing new registrations nationwide and imposing restrictive rules, aimed squarely at central Lisbon and Porto neighbourhoods where short-term rental density has been linked to rising housing costs for residents. Enforcement now runs to fines reported as high as 40,000 euros for unregistered operators. What has not changed is the food-and-drink price level, which remains the best argument for Porto over almost any comparable Western European city. Numbeo puts an inexpensive restaurant meal at about 8 euros, a francesinha, the city's gut-bomb signature sandwich, runs roughly 9 to 10 euros and up to 15 at tourist-facing places, a single metro ticket is 1.40 euros and an Andante Tour 24-hour pass is 7.50 euros. The climate is Atlantic rather than Mediterranean: roughly 1,146 to 1,237 mm of rain a year, summer averages of 16 to 26 C, winters of 5 to 15 C. Porto is a wet city, and visitors who book it expecting Algarve weather are the ones who leave disappointed.
destinations.what_great:
Porto is the rare European city where the famous view and the affordable meal are in the same neighbourhood. The Ribeira waterfront under the 1886 Dom Luis I Bridge is a genuinely great piece of urban landscape, the historic centre has been UNESCO-listed since 1996, and Sao Bento station is worth walking into even if you are not catching a train. Across the Douro, the Vila Nova de Gaia port lodges give you a serious, cheap, well-organised drinking education.

The economics still work in the visitor's favour. An inexpensive restaurant meal runs about 8 euros, a francesinha about 9 to 10, a metro ticket 1.40 euros and a 24-hour Andante Tour pass 7.50. For a UNESCO-listed Western European city with an airport handling 17 million passengers a year, that is an unusually low price floor, and it is why Porto keeps winning European Best Destination, in 2012, 2014 and 2017.
destinations.what_ruined:
Success is compressing a small city. Porto took more than 3 million tourists in 2025 against 2.8 million overnight visitors in 2017, funnelled into a steep, narrow historic core, and the government's own responses tell you how the pressure is being felt: the municipal tourist tax rose from about 2 to 3 euros per person per night capped at seven nights, 21 euros a trip, Vila Nova de Gaia across the river raised its own tax, and Portugal froze new alojamento local short-term rental registrations nationwide under the Mais Habitacao programme, with tightened oversight aimed specifically at central Lisbon and Porto where rental density has been tied to rising housing costs for residents. Fines for unregistered operators have been reported as high as 40,000 euros, which is worth knowing if you are booking something that looks informal.

The other honest warning is weather. Porto is Atlantic, not Mediterranean: about 1,146 to 1,237 mm of rain a year, summers averaging 16 to 26 C and winters 5 to 15 C. It is a genuinely rainy city, and people who book it as a beach-adjacent sun trip have misread the map.
tips: Budget the tourist tax separately. Porto charges about 3 euros per person per night, up from around 2, capped at seven nights for a maximum of 21 euros per trip, and Vila Nova de Gaia across the river has raised its own tax too.

Check that your rental is legally registered. Portugal froze new alojamento local registrations under the Mais Habitacao programme and fines for unregistered operators have been reported up to 40,000 euros.
Get the Andante Tour 24-hour pass at 7.50 euros if you plan more than five rides; single metro tickets are 1.40 euros.
Bring a rain jacket in any season. Porto gets roughly 1,146 to 1,237 mm of rain a year and is Atlantic, not Mediterranean.
Eat the francesinha away from the Ribeira waterfront. It runs about 9 to 10 euros at normal places and up to 15 at tourist-facing ones, for the same sandwich.
Sleep on the Gaia side if rates are better, but check its tourist tax before assuming it is cheaper; the port lodges and the bridge crossing are the reason many people stay there anyway.

guide.title: Porto Travel Guide: Taxes, Rentals, Transport and Rain in 2026
guide.summary: What Porto costs in 2026 after the tourist-tax increase and the short-term rental crackdown, plus how to get around a very steep small city.
guide.body:
Porto is cheap by Western European standards and the 2026 changes have not undone that, but they have added lines to the bill. The municipal tourist tax rose from around 2 euros to 3 euros per person per night, capped at seven nights, so no more than 21 euros per trip, with revenue directed at cultural heritage and infrastructure. Vila Nova de Gaia, the port-lodge side of the river where many visitors actually sleep, has raised its own tourist tax as well, so check which municipality your hotel is in before assuming the Gaia rate is lower. The bigger structural change is accommodation supply: Portugal's Mais Habitacao programme froze new alojamento local short-term rental registrations nationwide and tightened oversight of existing ones, with central Porto among the explicit targets because short-term rental density has been linked to rising housing costs for residents. Fines for unregistered operators have been reported as high as 40,000 euros, so book through platforms that display a valid AL registration number rather than an informal arrangement.

Day-to-day costs remain low. Numbeo puts an inexpensive restaurant meal at about 8 euros. A francesinha, the layered meat sandwich under melted cheese and beer sauce that Porto is known for, runs roughly 9 to 10 euros, or up to 15 in tourist-facing spots on the Ribeira. Transport is straightforward: a single metro ticket is 1.40 euros and the Andante Tour 24-hour pass is 7.50 euros, which pays for itself past about five rides. The city is small enough to walk, with the important caveat that it is built on a gorge, so almost every walk between the Ribeira waterfront and the upper town is a serious climb on granite that gets slippery when wet.

On timing, treat Porto as an Atlantic city. It gets roughly 1,146 to 1,237 mm of rain a year, with summer averages of 16 to 26 C and winters of 5 to 15 C, so it is mild year-round and wet in every season. Late spring and early autumn are the best combination of weather and crowd level; peak summer brings the bulk of the more than 3 million tourists the city took in 2025 into a historic centre that has been UNESCO-listed since 1996 and has not grown since. The core sights, the Ribeira, the 1886 Dom Luis I Bridge with its 172-metre span, Sao Bento station built between 1900 and 1916, and the Gaia port lodges, are all within a short radius of each other, which is a genuine advantage on a rainy day and a genuine problem in August.

rating_rationale.overall: A compact, beautiful, UNESCO-listed river city with an unusually low price floor for Western Europe, held short of a 5 by genuine crowding in a small historic core and by a wet Atlantic climate that surprises people.
rating_rationale.safety: Portugal is one of the safer countries in Europe for visitors, and Porto's issues are the standard urban ones, pickpocketing in the Ribeira and around Sao Bento and the tram routes, plus steep, slick granite steps that cause more visitor injuries than crime does.
rating_rationale.value: Genuinely cheap by Western European standards, an inexpensive meal about 8 euros, a francesinha 9 to 10, a metro ticket 1.40 and a 24-hour pass 7.50, with the main new cost being a tourist tax that rose to 3 euros per person per night capped at 21 euros per trip.

destinations.name: Prague
destinations.summary: Prague pairs a UNESCO listed historic core of Gothic, Baroque and Art Nouveau architecture with one of Europe's best beer and pub cultures, though rising visitor numbers pushed the city into new nightlife curfews, a tourist tax fight and a 2026 transit fare increase.
destinations.headline: Prague in 2026: Castle Views, Cheap Beer and a City Cracking Down on Overtourism
destinations.body:
Prague's historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992, remains one of the most architecturally intact old towns in Europe, with Gothic, Baroque and Art Nouveau buildings lining the Vltava River from Prague Castle down through Mala Strana, across Charles Bridge and into Old Town Square. St Vitus Cathedral and the Astronomical Clock anchor the main sightseeing route, while neighborhoods like Vinohrady and Zizkov offer quieter, residential alternatives with their own restaurant and pub scenes away from the main tourist flow.

The city is in the middle of a genuine crackdown on the effects of overtourism. As of January 1, 2026, shared e scooter rentals are banned citywide, organized bar crawls are prohibited between 10pm and 6am, and Prague 1 has designated no drinking zones covering Old Town Square, the Charles Bridge area and Wenceslas Square, where an open container can draw a fine. Prague's municipal tourist tax currently sits at CZK 50 per person per night, but Prague 1's district council has proposed raising it to roughly CZK 175, about EUR 7, to bring it closer to the EU average. A national review board is expected to rule by mid 2026, with any new rate taking effect in 2027.

Getting around got more expensive at the start of 2026. A 30 minute PID transit ticket now costs 39 CZK on paper, or 36 CZK in the PID Litacka app, and a 90 minute ticket costs 50 CZK on paper, or 46 CZK in app, both covering metro, tram, bus and the Petrin funicular with a single validation. The Airport Express bus from Vaclav Havel Airport to Prague's main train station also doubled in price in January 2026, from 100 to 200 CZK for the roughly 35 minute ride.

A day trip to Kutna Hora, about one hour away by train, remains one of the best side trips from Prague, combining the Gothic St Barbara's Cathedral with the Sedlec Ossuary, a chapel decorated with the bones of an estimated 40,000 to 70,000 people. Visitors from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and dozens of other visa exempt countries can currently stay up to 90 days within any 180 day period without a visa. The EU's ETIAS pre travel authorization system is expected to start applying to this group in late 2026.
destinations.what_great: Prague's core appeal is architectural density paired with an unusually good and still affordable food and beer scene. Czech pilsner style lager, hearty pub fare and a real neighborhood life in areas like Vinohrady and Zizkov reward visitors who venture beyond Old Town. The castle complex, Charles Bridge and the Vltava riverfront deliver on the postcard version of the city, and Kutna Hora offers one of the more unusual and worthwhile day trips in Central Europe.
destinations.what_ruined: The honest friction is overcrowding and rising cost. Old Town Square, Charles Bridge and the routes between them are jammed with tour groups for much of the year, and the same few blocks host currency exchange counters running bait and switch rates plus restaurants that pad bills with unlisted service charges, uninvited bread baskets and tip screens defaulting to 20 percent. Transit fares and the airport bus both got meaningfully more expensive in January 2026, and the city's own fight over its tourist tax signals further increases are coming for 2027.
tips: A 90 minute Prague public transit ticket covering metro, tram and bus costs 50 CZK on paper or 46 CZK in the PID Litacka app as of the January 2026 fare increase, and must be validated once at the start of the trip.

The Airport Express bus from Vaclav Havel Airport to Praha hlavni nadrazi costs 200 CZK one way as of January 2026, after the fare was doubled from 100 CZK. Regular Prague transit tickets are not valid on this line.

Prague Castle's main Circuit ticket, covering the Old Royal Palace, St George's Basilica, Golden Lane and St Vitus Cathedral interior, costs 450 CZK for an adult and 300 CZK for a concession. The castle grounds and courtyards are free and open daily from 6am to 10pm.

Citizens of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and roughly 55 other visa exempt countries can stay in the Czech Republic and the wider Schengen area for up to 90 days within any 180 day period without a visa.

At ATMs and card terminals in Prague, always choose to be charged in CZK rather than accepting the machine's offered home currency conversion, known as Dynamic Currency Conversion, which typically carries a 3 to 7 percent hidden markup.
Prague's shared e scooter rental services have been banned citywide since January 1, 2026, and organized bar crawls are prohibited between 10pm and 6am under new city rules.

guide.title: Prague Travel Guide 2026: When to Go, Where to Stay and What to Skip
guide.summary: A practical primer on visiting Prague in 2026, covering transit costs, neighborhood choices, day trips and the scams worth knowing about before landing.
guide.body:
Most visitors fly into Vaclav Havel Airport and take the Airport Express bus, 200 CZK, about 35 minutes, or a metro plus tram combination into the center. Ride hailing apps such as Bolt and Uber are widely available and often cheaper than a taxi hailed at the terminal. Spring, April through June, and early autumn, September and October, offer the best balance of mild weather and manageable crowds, while July and August bring peak heat and the heaviest tour group traffic through Old Town Square and Charles Bridge. Winter is cold but quiet, and Prague Castle's interiors keep shorter hours, 9am to 4pm, from November through March.

For lodging, Old Town and Mala Strana put visitors inside walking distance of the major sights but at premium prices and maximum foot traffic. Vinohrady and Zizkov, both a short tram ride from the center, offer quieter, more residential stays with strong local restaurant and pub scenes at lower cost. Budget travelers can expect to spend meaningfully less than in Paris or Amsterdam, though the January 2026 transit fare increase and the proposed 2027 tourist tax hike are narrowing that gap.

A single 90 minute PID transit ticket, 50 CZK on paper or 46 CZK via the PID Litacka app, covers the metro, trams and buses citywide and must be validated once at the start of the ride. Must do sightseeing includes Prague Castle and St Vitus Cathedral, the Astronomical Clock in Old Town Square, and an early morning walk across Charles Bridge before the crowds arrive. A worthwhile day trip is Kutna Hora, about one hour away by train, for the Sedlec Ossuary and St Barbara's Cathedral. What to avoid: currency exchange counters and restaurants directly on Old Town Square, Charles Bridge and Wenceslas Square, where bait exchange rates and padded restaurant bills are well documented. Eating and exchanging money one street back, on streets such as Dlouha or Dusni, avoids most of it.

rating_rationale.overall: Prague delivers fully on its architectural and cultural reputation, but heavy crowding in the historic core and a fast changing fee landscape keep it just short of a perfect score.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime against tourists is rare in Prague, but well documented currency exchange and restaurant overcharging scams are frequent enough in the main tourist zones to warrant real caution.
rating_rationale.value: Prague remains cheaper than most Western European capitals, but the January 2026 transit fare hike, the doubled airport bus fare and a looming tourist tax increase are steadily narrowing that gap.

facts_checked: Prague's municipal tourist tax is currently CZK 50 per person per night; Prague 1's district council has proposed raising it to about CZK 175, roughly EUR 7, with a national decision expected by mid 2026 and a new rate effective 2027 if approved. Source: expats.cz coverage of the Prague 1 tourist tax proposal.

Shared e scooter rentals have been banned citywide since January 1, 2026; organized bar crawls are banned between 10pm and 6am; no drinking zones now cover Old Town Square, the Charles Bridge area and Wenceslas Square. Source: 2026 Prague overtourism coverage on bestpragueguide.com and dreamville.cz.

The 30 minute PID transit ticket costs 39 CZK on paper or 36 CZK in the PID Litacka app; the 90 minute ticket costs 50 CZK on paper or 46 CZK in app, effective January 1, 2026. Source: e15.cz Czech finance and transit reporting on the 2026 PID fare increase.
The Airport Express bus fare was doubled from 100 CZK to 200 CZK in January 2026, for the roughly 35 minute ride from the airport to Praha hlavni nadrazi with no transfers. Source: Prague Daily News.

Prague Castle's Circuit ticket costs 450 CZK for an adult, 300 CZK concession, 950 CZK for a family; the Tower of the Cathedral view gallery costs 200 CZK for an adult; the grounds are free and open daily 6am to 10pm, with interiors open 9am to 5pm in summer and 9am to 4pm in winter. Source: timetravelturtle.com and thebettervacation.com 2026 Prague Castle ticket guides.

Visa exempt visitors, including from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, may stay up to 90 days within any 180 day period in the Schengen area including Czechia; the EU's ETIAS pre travel authorization is expected to begin applying to this group in late 2026. Source: europe-visa.eu and axa-schengen.com.

Currency exchange scams are common near Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, and ATM Dynamic Currency Conversion carries a 3 to 7 percent markup; travelers should always choose to be charged in CZK. Source: bestpragueguide.com Prague scams guide.
