destinations.name: Zanzibar
destinations.summary: Stunning beaches and a UNESCO old town, but a stack of new taxes, a mandatory e-visa, and a real land-rights fight behind the resort boom.
destinations.headline: Zanzibar in 2026: gorgeous beaches, a UNESCO old town, and a growing pile of fees and friction
destinations.body:
Zanzibar had a record year. The archipelago logged 917,167 international arrivals in 2025, up nearly 25 percent from 736,755 in 2024, and European travelers, led by Italy at roughly 14 percent of visitors followed by France and Poland, now dominate the mix. That surge is exactly why the honest version of this trip looks different than it did a few years ago: more fees, more construction, and more scrutiny of who actually benefits from the boom.

Start with entry. As of January 2025, Tanzania scrapped visa on arrival entirely. Every visitor now needs an e-visa applied for in advance at visa.immigration.go.tz, a single-entry tourist e-visa runs about $50 for up to 90 days, and US citizens specifically are pushed into the $100 multiple-entry visa even for a one-time trip. Processing typically takes two to five business days, so this is not something to leave for the airport.

Once you land, the fees keep stacking. Zanzibar's hotel infrastructure levy, essentially a bed-night tax, jumped from $5 to $10 per person per night as of August 1, 2024, approved by the Zanzibar House of Representatives and charged on every overnight stay (day-trippers are exempt). Then, starting November 1, 2025, a new international flight tax of $45 one-way or $90 round-trip gets folded directly into airline ticket prices for anyone flying in or out, funding passenger-data systems the government says will improve travel security. None of this is disclosed clearly upfront in most vacation-package marketing.

The development story underneath the tourism numbers is more uncomfortable. Zanzibar's parliament spent much of 2025 airing land disputes publicly: lawmakers accused government officials of fueling forged titles and multiple-ownership claims, and criticized the government for failing to compensate residents displaced when their homes were demolished for infrastructure projects. In September 2025, fourteen international scientists wrote an open letter urging Zanzibar's government to relocate a planned luxury resort on Pemba island away from an ecologically sensitive reserve, and as of March 2026 construction was reportedly continuing despite the objections. A separate, widely covered dispute saw a British developer accuse Zanzibar authorities of undermining a planned beach resort without due process. None of this means don't go. It means the beachfront resort you're booking sits inside a live, unresolved fight over who controls Zanzibar's coastline.

Health-wise, malaria risk is high across all of Tanzania below 1,800 meters, including the entire Zanzibar archipelago, so prophylaxis (atovaquone/proguanil, doxycycline, or mefloquine) is genuinely worth arranging with a doctor before you go, not an optional extra. Yellow fever vaccination is only mandatory if you're arriving from, or transiting more than 12 hours through, a country with yellow fever risk; travelers flying direct from the US or Europe typically don't need it. On safety, the US State Department raised its overall Tanzania travel advisory to Level 3, Reconsider Travel, on October 31, 2025, citing crime, unrest, terrorism concentrated in the Mtwara region on the southern mainland, and targeting of LGBTQ+ travelers by police. Zanzibar itself sits hundreds of kilometers from that flashpoint and is generally described as calmer than the mainland, but the advisory covers the whole country and same-sex sexual conduct remains criminalized, which matters for how openly LGBTQ+ travelers can move.
destinations.what_great:
Stone Town is a genuine UNESCO World Heritage Site, a dense old quarter of coral-stone buildings and more than a thousand carved wooden doors that eight centuries of Swahili, Arab, Persian, Indian, and European trade actually built, not a themed recreation of one. Spice tours through working plantations that still grow clove, nutmeg, cinnamon, and vanilla, the crops that made 19th-century Zanzibar the world's largest clove producer, run roughly $15 to $40 and are a real agricultural visit rather than a gift-shop stop.

The beaches on the east coast and around Nungwi are the reason nearly a million people visited in 2025, and the tourism sector is large enough now that flights, resorts, and dive operators are well developed and easy to book. For travelers who want turquoise water and a walkable historic town in the same trip, few places in East Africa pair the two as directly as Zanzibar does.
destinations.what_ruined:
The fee stack is the honest headline. Between the mandatory $50 to $100 e-visa, the $10-per-person-per-night hotel levy added on top of your room rate since August 2024, and the new $45 to $90 international flight tax layered into airfare from November 2025, a couple can easily add several hundred dollars in government charges to a one-week trip, most of it not obvious from the advertised price. Malaria prophylaxis and, for some itineraries, yellow fever vaccination add planning overhead and cost most beach-vacation marketing glosses over.

The bigger issue is what's happening behind the beachfront. Zanzibar's own lawmakers spent 2025 publicly describing a land administration system riddled with forged titles and disputed ownership, with residents displaced for infrastructure projects and, by the government's own lawmakers' account, often left uncompensated. International scientists and at least one foreign developer have separately accused authorities of pushing resort development forward, including on an ecologically sensitive reserve, over documented objections. Book a beach resort here and there's a real chance it sits on land whose ownership history would not survive a close look. Tanzania's mainland is also under a US Level 3 advisory for crime and terrorism risk as of October 2025, and while Zanzibar itself is calmer, that context is part of the same country you're flying into.
tips: Apply for Tanzania's e-visa in advance at visa.immigration.go.tz; visa on arrival was abolished in January 2025 and processing takes 2 to 5 business days.
Budget an extra $10 per person, per night for Zanzibar's hotel infrastructure levy, in effect since August 1, 2024, on top of your quoted room rate.
Check your return airfare includes the international departure tax (about $45 one-way, $90 round-trip) that airlines began folding into ticket prices from November 1, 2025.
Start malaria prophylaxis (atovaquone/proguanil, doxycycline, or mefloquine) before you go; risk is high across the entire archipelago, and there is no vaccine.
US citizens need Tanzania's $100 multiple-entry e-visa even for a single trip, not the standard $50 single-entry visa other nationalities can use.
Ask directly where a beachfront resort's land title comes from before booking; Zanzibar's own parliament flagged widespread forged and disputed land titles in 2025.

guide.title: Zanzibar Travel Guide: Getting In, Getting Around, and What It Actually Costs
guide.summary: Practical logistics for Zanzibar in 2026, from the mandatory e-visa to which coast to base yourself on and how to dodge the worst of the new fees.
guide.body:
Most international flights land at Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ) outside Stone Town, either direct on charter and leisure carriers from Europe or via a connection through Dar es Salaam or Nairobi. Have your e-visa approval printed or saved before you fly since Tanzania stopped issuing visas on arrival in January 2025; applying at visa.immigration.go.tz two to five business days ahead avoids any airport surprises. Getting around the island itself is mostly by private taxi or a hotel-arranged transfer for the roughly 45 minute to hour-long drive from the airport to the east-coast beach areas, with dala-dala shared minibuses the cheap but slow local option and rental scooters or cars an option for confident, experienced drivers used to left-hand traffic and minimal signage.

Stone Town is the obvious base if you want to walk to the House of Wonders, the Old Fort, and the old slave market site, and stay amid the carved-door architecture that earned the district its UNESCO listing. It's also the most urban, least beach-adjacent option. The east coast, around Paje, Jambiani, and Bwejuu, has the calmer, powder-sand beaches and is the kitesurfing hub, while Nungwi and Kendwa on the northern tip have livelier resort strips and some of the best swimming since they're less affected by the tide going out over reef flats than the east coast can be.

On timing, Zanzibar's tourism numbers have been climbing steadily, with October 2025 arrivals up 24 percent year over year and December 2025 up another 10 percent, so the traditional dry, high-season months from roughly June through October and December through February are getting busier and pricier each year. The long rains typically fall March through May, which is the quietest and cheapest window if you can tolerate more rain and humidity in exchange for thinner crowds and lower rates.

On money, budget beyond the room rate itself. The $10-per-person, per-night hotel levy introduced in August 2024 and the international flight tax that started folding into airfares in November 2025 aren't always itemized clearly by booking sites, so ask your hotel or airline directly what's included before you commit. Spice tours ($15 to $40) and Stone Town's museums are inexpensive relative to a full day on the water, so if the budget is tight, prioritize a spice tour and a couple of Stone Town half-days over stacking multiple paid excursions.

rating_rationale.overall: World-class beaches and a genuine UNESCO old town, undercut by an unresolved land-rights fight over the same coastline being marketed to tourists.
rating_rationale.safety: Zanzibar itself is calmer than mainland Tanzania, but the country carries a US Level 3 advisory since Oct 31, 2025 for crime, unrest and terrorism risk, plus real legal risk for LGBTQ+ travelers.
rating_rationale.value: A mandatory $50-100 e-visa, a $10/person/night hotel levy since Aug 2024, and a new $45-90 flight tax from Nov 2025 stack fees most travelers don't see until they're already booked.

destinations.name: Zurich
destinations.summary: Zurich delivers Swiss efficiency and free lake and river swimming, but a franc at an 11 year high against the dollar in 2026 makes nearly everything else genuinely expensive.
destinations.headline: Zurich in 2026: Free Lake Swims, Punctual Trams, and a Franc So Strong Everything Else Feels Pricier
destinations.body:
Zurich is Switzerland's largest city and its financial capital, sitting at the northwestern tip of Lake Zurich where the Limmat river flows out past the old town's Lindenhof hill. It is also, by wide reputation, one of the priciest destinations in the world, a status driven less by any single expensive attraction and more by the combined weight of Swiss wages, Swiss real estate, and a currency that keeps getting stronger. The Swiss franc gained 12.7 percent against the US dollar in 2025 alone, and by January 2026 it had appreciated a further 3.5 percent year to date, pushing it to an eleven year high. That strength, paired with an unfavorable exchange rate against the euro as well, is exactly what travel guides point to when they describe Switzerland as one of the priciest countries to visit on the continent. A traveler converting dollars or euros into francs in 2026 is simply getting fewer francs for the same money than a few years ago, and every price in Zurich, already high in franc terms, compounds that squeeze.

Public transport is the one place where Zurich's cost curve bends back in the traveler's favor, at least relative to what it delivers. The city center sits inside ZVV zone 110, and a single ticket there costs 6.80 francs, the same fare that covers the airport train into the main station, so arriving travelers are not paying extra just to get downtown. That fare buys a system of trams, buses, S-Bahn trains, and even boats, unified enough that one zone based ticket works across all of them, and reliable enough that Zurich is regularly cited for some of the best on time performance of any public transport network in the world. The tram network alone runs sixteen lines across 185 stops and carries roughly 200 million passengers a year, part of a wider ZVV system moving more than 1.3 million riders a day and over 500 million a year. Travelers who plan to move around a lot can compare day cards against single fares, or use the discounted 9-UhrPass for trips starting after 9am, and the paid Zurich Card layers on free museum entry plus further transit discounts, though it is an add on purchase rather than something included automatically.

The lake and river culture is the other side of Zurich that softens the sticker shock, because unlike almost everything else in the city, it is genuinely free. The public river baths at Oberer and Unterer Letten let anyone swim in the clean, fast moving Limmat at no charge, and the Frauenbad Stadthausquai, a women only floating bathhouse on the lake, provides showers and free lockers, asking only that visitors bring their own padlock. On a warm afternoon these spots fill with locals treating a swim as a normal part of the day, not a special outing, and it is one of the clearest windows into how Zurich residents actually live rather than how the city markets itself to tourists.

None of that changes the basic math for anyone visiting in 2026. Museum tickets run into the mid teens of francs, a zoo visit costs 26 francs for an adult, and even theater seats marketed as a bargain still run 20 francs for last minute rush tickets. Add a currency near an eleven year high and the arithmetic gets harder with every purchase. Zurich rewards travelers who plan around its free assets, the lake, the river, and the walkable old town, and who budget deliberately for the parts that are not free, rather than those who assume any single price they see will be the last surprise of the trip.
destinations.what_great:
Zurich pairs efficient, punctual public transport, trams, buses, and S-Bahn trains unified under the ZVV zone system, with genuinely free public spaces that most expensive cities do not offer. The free river baths at Oberer and Unterer Letten and the Frauenbad Stadthausquai floating bathhouse let visitors swim in the Limmat and Lake Zurich at no cost, a real counterweight to how expensive everything else is. The old town around Lindenhof hill is compact and walkable, and the transit network's reliability means visitors rarely lose time waiting on connections.

A strong, safe haven franc is good news for anyone earning in francs and for price stability, since the currency tends to hold its value rather than swing wildly, and museum culture is dense enough, the Landesmuseum and Kunsthaus among them, that a short stay can be filled without needing a car.
destinations.what_ruined:
The Swiss franc's strength is the single biggest friction point for anyone converting from dollars or euros. After gaining 12.7 percent against the dollar in 2025 and pushing to an eleven year high by January 2026, every purchase in Zurich effectively got more expensive for outside visitors even where local prices did not change. A single tram ticket at 6.80 francs, a zoo visit at 26 francs, or museum admission in the mid teens of francs all add up fast, and there is no simple workaround since food, hotels, and transit all sit on the same high wage, high cost foundation.

Travelers expecting a free transit card automatically included with a hotel stay, a system some other Swiss resort towns use, should not assume one exists in Zurich specifically, since no such city wide program turned up in official transit or tourism sources. Budget travelers will need to lean hard on the free river baths and walking the old town to keep costs in check, because there are few genuinely cheap options once meals and paid attractions enter the picture.
tips: A single ZVV ticket in downtown zone 110 costs 6.80 francs, the same fare that covers the airport train into the main station, so budget the same amount whether you are crossing town or arriving from the airport.

Swim for free at the public river baths at Oberer and Unterer Letten on the Limmat, or at the women only Frauenbad Stadthausquai floating bathhouse on the lake, which has free lockers but requires you to bring your own padlock.

The Swiss franc hit an eleven year high against the dollar by January 2026 after gaining 12.7 percent through 2025, so convert money expecting every price to feel more expensive than it did even a year earlier.
If your schedule allows a later start, buy the 9-UhrPass instead of a standard day card, since it is discounted specifically for travel beginning after 9am.

Do not assume a free transit card comes automatically with a hotel stay in Zurich the way it does in some Swiss resort towns; no such city wide program is documented, so budget for tickets or a day card separately.
Museum admission runs from about 13 francs at the Landesmuseum to 16 francs at the Kunsthaus, and the paid Zurich Card bundles free museum entry with transit discounts if you plan to visit several.

guide.title: Zurich Travel Guide: Getting Around, When to Go, and How to Not Overspend
guide.summary: A practical guide to navigating Zurich's transit system, timing a visit, and finding the city's free lake and river swimming spots.
guide.body:
Zurich's ZVV network is the backbone of getting around, and it is worth understanding zones before buying anything. Downtown Zurich sits in zone 110, and a single ticket there costs 6.80 francs, the same fare that covers the airport train into the main station, so there is no separate premium for arriving travelers. Trams and buses run on the same zone based tickets as the S-Bahn trains, and the network is dense enough, sixteen tram lines across 185 stops, that most of the city center and inner neighborhoods are reachable without a car. Travelers doing more than a couple of rides a day should compare a 24 hour day card against buying single tickets, and anyone whose plans start later in the morning can save with the 9-UhrPass, discounted for travel beginning after 9am.

Money moves in one direction only in 2026, and that is toward the franc being worth more, not less. The currency gained close to 13 percent against the dollar through 2025 and kept climbing into an eleven year high by January 2026, so converting cash earlier in a trip rather than later, and expecting every price to feel a bit more expensive than it did a year or two ago, is the realistic approach.

The old town clusters around Lindenhof hill on the west bank of the Limmat, walkable enough that a first time visitor can cover most of the historic core on foot in a day, with St. Peter's church and the Town Hall as easy anchors. For a genuinely free afternoon, head to the public river baths at Oberer or Unterer Letten for a swim in the Limmat, or to the Frauenbad Stadthausquai floating bathhouse on the lake, which provides showers and free lockers to anyone who brings a padlock. Summer, when the water and the free bathing spots are actually usable, is the season that makes Zurich's cost of living feel least punishing, since the best neighborhood tradition in the city does not require a franc.

rating_rationale.overall: Efficient transit and free lake and river swimming offset a genuinely high cost of living, but nearly every paid experience carries a premium.
rating_rationale.safety: Switzerland's 2024 homicide rate of about 0.5 per 100,000 people is among the lowest in the world, per Wikipedia's crime data for the country.
rating_rationale.value: A franc at an 11 year high against the dollar as of January 2026, combined with consistently high franc denominated prices for museums, food, and tickets, makes Zurich a poor value city despite its free swimming spots and reliable transit.

facts_checked: Zurich's population was 436,551 at the end of 2024 (Wikipedia)
Zurich's urban area population was 1.45 million in 2020 and its metro area was 2.1 million (Wikipedia)
Downtown Zurich is ZVV fare zone 110 and a single ticket there costs 6.80 francs (Wikivoyage)
The airport train to Zurich main station also costs 6.80 francs (Wikivoyage)

Zurich's ZVV network moves over 1.3 million riders daily and over 500 million annually; the tram network has 16 lines across 185 stops carrying about 200 million passengers a year (Wikipedia, Public transport in Zurich)
Zurich is regularly cited for some of the best on time public transport performance in the world (Wikipedia, Public transport in Zurich)
Free public river baths exist at Oberer and Unterer Letten on the Limmat; the Frauenbad Stadthausquai is a women only floating bathhouse with free lockers (Wikivoyage)
The Swiss franc gained 12.7 percent against the US dollar in 2025 and rose a further 3.5 percent year to date by January 2026, reaching an 11 year high (Wikipedia, Swiss franc)
Switzerland's 2024 homicide rate was about 0.5 per 100,000 people, among the lowest in the world (Wikipedia, Crime in Switzerland)
Museum admission cited at roughly 13 francs for the Landesmuseum and 16 francs for the Kunsthaus; zoo entry is 26 francs for adults (Wikivoyage)
Wikivoyage describes Switzerland as one of the priciest destinations in the world due to high costs and an unfavorable exchange rate, especially against the euro
